Compute off-shell one-loop two-point functions in general d, extract momentum-dependent kinetic corrections, and sum interacting tower states below the species cutoff. Modulus vertices follow from mass derivatives: λn=2mn∂φmn and μn=∂φmn.

Use string/M-theory dualities and dimensional reduction for tower content and gravitino–form couplings. The c-map and Poisson resummation relate hypermultiplet D-instanton sums to particle-loop/KK descriptions.

Higher gauging inserts symmetry-defect networks on a submanifold. For the specified discrete torsion, magnetic×winding 1-gauging produces a trivial closed condensation defect; imposing Dirichlet conditions on a boundary yields D^(1)_{p/N}. The authors use this construction to establish topologicality and determine defect actions.

Dress anomalous symmetry operators with lower-dimensional TQFTs: the shift defect uses a 2+1-dimensional minimal Z_N TQFT, while the electric surface uses 1+1-dimensional Z_N gauge theory with compact scalar φ and U(1) connection c coupled to θ and F.

Use anomalous symmetry-line fusion to derive modular phases, then relate twisted/twined genera to topological strings with fractional B-fields. B-brane autoequivalences provide an intersection-theoretic route to the modular transformations.
Construct rank-three monad bundles as kernels between sums of line bundles; realize their Calabi–Yau hypersurfaces through toric complete intersections and calculate spectra and intersection data.

Evaluate fermionic eta invariants on the lens-space generator of Omega_7^Spin(BZ_3)=Z_9, subtract pure gravitational contributions, and describe self-dual tensors through seven-dimensional three-form fields in differential cohomology.

Regularity is analyzed separately near each bubble using local spherical coordinates. Removing conical singularities fixes circle periodicities; integrals of F₃ over the outer bolts determine opposite quantized five-brane charges.

The construction uses an imported integrable supergravity formalism: with D−2 commuting Killing vectors and suitable fluxes, the governing equations decompose into Ernst equations. The Letter presents the solution while deferring construction details to a companion paper.

Reduction along (x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄,x₅,y) gives a geometry with R^{3,1} asymptotics. Its ADM mass, expressed per unit x₁x₂x₃ volume, is compared with wrapped BPS five-brane masses to analyze an emission channel.

Canonical normalization and orthonormal field transformations identify exponential rates. No-go identities select particular field directions; Bianchi identities and tadpole cancellation determine whether apparently problematic negative terms can dominate.
The authors integrate FLRW inequalities, express logarithmic changes of |V| as field-interval averages, and apply Cauchy–Schwarz to definite Riemann integrals to obtain the second-derivative bound.

Mandelstam double-spectral representations organize single and double discontinuities. Regge subtraction and continuously weighted dispersion relations yield finite-energy and continuous-moment sum rules.

Wigner partial waves are reorganized into Chebyshev multipoles with nonnegative spectral weights. Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities, Hankel moment determinants and finite-multipole linear optimization produce coefficient bounds.
Crossing-symmetric dispersion relations expand the amplitude at fixed a=y/x. Locality removes spurious inverse powers of x, generating null constraints on positive spectral densities.

Smearing preserves integrated source normalization. On-shell action terms are evaluated through pure-spinor identities and supersymmetry conditions, allowing delta-function coefficients to be extracted without constructing the localized geometry.

Pure-spinor supersymmetry equations are related to generalized F- and D-flatness. Localized corrections are motivated by the Veneziano–Yankielowicz superpotential, quadratic D-brane gaugino couplings and consistency with RR and NSNS flux equations.
Compute circle-reduction anomaly inflow through one-loop Chern–Simons terms, using KK anomaly polynomials, regularized sums, η invariants and the APS index theorem.
Use imported bordism computations and the Cobordism Conjecture to identify a reflection-monodromy class requiring an additional defect.
Analyze asymptotic monodromies, Killing-spinor boundary conditions and brane-junction lassos; shrinking a lasso converts its excess asymptotic charge into charge ending on the defect.
Test possible inflow couplings by polynomial factorization and preserved-reflection parity. This identifies candidate cancellation channels without establishing their existence or normalization.
Regularize the sum of massive KK anomaly polynomials or integrate the circle eta form, retaining spin structure, mass signs, and possible zero-mode contributions.

Compute horizon luminosity from the inflaton stress tensor, integrate the approximate static-Killing current over the future horizon, and use the near-Killing-horizon Raychaudhuri equation to relate flux to horizon-area growth and the first law.

Impose static-time diffeomorphism invariance through an invariant operator subalgebra and gravitational dressing. Use relative Tomita/modular operators, the Connes cocycle, and relative entropy to construct an approximate density matrix and interpret its entropy.

The reviewed island method uses generalized entropy S_gen = [k c^3/(4Gℏ)] A(X) + S_bulk, with X a quantum extremal surface and S_bulk the entropy of a region bounded by X. The overview instructs taking an extremal value; k denotes Boltzmann's constant.

The S-matrix bootstrap constrains theories and admissible EFTs using causality, analyticity and unitarity. The cosmological bootstrap extends this approach toward model-independent properties of inflation and de Sitter space; the review describes that extension as still developing.

The computational survey names machine learning, genetic algorithms and related techniques for studying string models, reporting progress on Calabi–Yau metrics and systematic construction of exponentially small superpotentials. No algorithms or accuracy estimates are supplied here.

Vacuum-energy arguments use worldline and torus partition functions, modular regularization and microscopic state counting matched to gravitational entropy. The metaparticle path integral uses the commuting (x,p̃) polarization; causal proper-time integration is positive, while the second constraint parameter ranges over the full real line.

The axilaton analysis solves coupled Einstein–axion-dilaton equations using a codimension-two warped metric, axial metric symmetry and τ=τ(θ). Warp factors are expanded perturbatively in anisotropy ω, with displayed remainders O(ω⁴), and compared with global cosmic-brane solutions.

Use the D4-sourced F4 Bianchi identity to describe a flux jump across a brane. With transverse backreaction suppressed or the brane effectively smeared over the flux four-cycle, the solution has the step-function form F4=[N+Q_D4 θ(y)]ε4.

Expand the D4 DBI action to obtain the position-scalar kinetic metric, combine it with dilaton and volume kinetic terms, and solve a reduced geodesic problem. Using D=φ−Σ_iσ_i and z=e^(−D/2), the symmetric field space becomes H2×R, with circular geodesics in the hyperbolic coordinates.

Worldsheet methods include Faddeev–Popov gauge fixing, matter/ghost central-charge accounting, BRST cohomology, light-cone quantization, modular invariance and genus-expanded correlation functions integrated over worldsheet moduli.

Geometric methods include holonomy tests for parallel spinors and ADE intersection matrices. Supersymmetric minimal models and a U(1) gauged linear sigma model are introduced to relate Landau–Ginzburg descriptions to Calabi–Yau sigma models; the supplied setup does not contain the intervening phase analysis.

Solve hypergeometric Picard–Fuchs equations, match local solutions numerically to an integral symplectic period basis, and evaluate BPS masses M=|Z|. Numerical scans and local period expansions locate minima of F1 and compare selected BPS gaps.

Motivate species counting through weighted determinants of Laplacians on (p,q)-forms and through higher-derivative curvature/dilaton couplings analogous to the CFT a-function. The latter is an on-shell analogy, rather than conformal anomaly matching in gravity.

Integrate the genus-one holomorphic anomaly using the Kähler potential, metric determinant, and holomorphic ambiguity. Boundary asymptotics fix the ambiguity in the examples; conifold coefficients change from 1/12 to |G|/12 for a shrinking Lens space S³/G.

Compute a covariant derivative of an OPE coefficient on the conformal manifold using the regularised integral of a connected four-point function. At leading large N, the required integrand is determined by Wick contractions of O and χ.

Regularise with a hard-sphere cutoff: excise small discs, subtract only divergent terms and take the cutoff to zero. Radial integration and hypergeometric identities produce the finite result in the stated minimal-subtraction scheme.

Count powers of N in connected single-trace correlators and Wick contractions of multi-trace constituents. Unsuppressed connected multi-trace contributions are used to alter selected single-trace correlators while retaining a convergent large-N expansion.

Infer NS5 corrections by completing D5 corrections in gs using a proposed Eisenstein-series dependence, then S-dualizing. Naive S-dualization of tree-level D5 terms gives different gs scaling because duality exchanges perturbative orders and nonperturbative contributions.

Numerically map metastable minima and fit the zero-energy locus. Reformulate the LVS Parametric Tadpole Constraint using ce=gsM, the bulk-warping control parameter cN, and the −1 branch of Lambert W, then evaluate selected model parameters.

Evaluate known DBI and Chern–Simons curvature/flux couplings at the KS tip. Tangential covariant constancy and allowed normal/tangential index structures eliminate many terms; surviving couplings are combined into Vtot=VKPV+Vcurv+Vflux.

Decompose bosonic fields into polarization tensors and fermionic fields into spinors times polarization tensors with Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. Longitudinal momentum contractions generate Legendre polynomials Ps, supplying explicit spin-dependent angular factors.

Numerically integrate the bosonic and fermionic angular recoil expressions in Mathematica. Compare normalized angular maps and momentum-dependent amplitudes, including scans over representative integer spins and corresponding fermionic cases.

Calculate mediator-exchange amplitudes, expand spinor bilinears in the nonrelativistic limit and form polarization-dependent squared amplitudes. Fold the cross sections with the halo velocity distribution, using the recoil delta function to perform the speed integral.

F-theory uses Weierstrass models, Kodaira singularities and monodromies: codimension-one, two and three loci encode non-abelian gauge algebras, localised matter and Yukawa interactions. Gauge backgrounds require finer data than field strength alone, described through Deligne cohomology and partly through Chow groups.

RCFT construction uses c=9, N=2 minimal-model tensor products, simple-current modular invariants, and boundary/crosscap coefficients. Annulus and Möbius amplitudes determine spectra; axion mixing, tadpoles and global anomalies require further checks. Boundary completeness is explicitly presented as a conjecture.

Topological chiral-index computations: D6-branes use the signed intersection I_ab=[Π_a]·[Π_b]; fluxed D7-branes use Riemann–Roch–Hirzebruch and divisor/flux intersections. In F-theory, χ(R)=n_R−n_R̄=∫_{S_R}G4 over a matter surface.

Functional renormalization group studies use the scale-dependent effective action Γk to search for ultraviolet fixed points and connect them to infrared phenomenology. Truncations commonly retain interactions ordered by canonical dimension.

Background-field and fluctuation computations distinguish background from fluctuation couplings. A linear metric split does not require small fluctuations; the background approximation identifies corresponding couplings and neglects nontrivial dependence constrained by Nielsen identities.

Crossing-derived null constraints and nonnegative partial-wave spectral weights are combined with FESRs. Bounds follow by adding positive multiples of null polynomials, separating small and large spins, relaxing large spin to a continuous variable, and optimizing auxiliary parameters numerically or through small-ε approximations.

Finite complex-contour moments of M(s,t)(s+t/2)^(2n+1) connect absorptive integrals below M* to a Regge approximation on an upper semicircle centered at s=-t/2. Analyticity outside the contour is explicitly unnecessary.

Evaluate H(N)-derivative expressions for slow-roll parameters and use ns = 1 − 6ε + 2η and r = 16ε. Reconstruct potential-derivative bounds as functions of ns and r, then plot C1 and C2 for selected negative and nonnegative powers n.

Background reconstruction: specify H, solve the extended mimetic equations for V and the Lagrange multiplier, express them in e-fold time N, and obtain V(φ) using dN/dt = H and φ = t. The paper also outlines reconstruction through g(t) = df_G/dt.

Integrate over throat modulus b and U(N) holonomy eigenvalues. The effective action combines JT gravity φr b²/(2πL), Weyl anomaly bN/24, a holonomy-dependent Casimir term, and logarithmic eigenvalue repulsion from the Haar measure. Large-N eigenvalue density and the b saddle are solved together.

The eigenvalue saddle is parametrized by its support endpoint θc using an imported matrix-model solution. Fourier sums are evaluated semi-analytically with Appell F1 functions and asymptotic subtraction; the reported numerical illustration truncates at nmax=200.

Functional renormalization group: project the effective-action flow onto retained operators to obtain beta functions. The formally exact flow has a one-loop structure but is not restricted to one-loop perturbation theory. The implementation uses a flat Euclidean background, Landau gauge with α = β = 0, a Litim regulator and a vertex expansion.

Search for common beta-function zeros, linearize around candidates and examine critical exponents; integrate RG flows to connect UV and IR coupling intervals. Separately, solve the scalar equation of motion together with present-day equation-of-state and density constraints, then constrain solutions using the braiding parameter.

The neutrino analysis uses an infinite KK decomposition and Dirac mass matrix, with volume-suppressed brane–bulk masses m_i^D ≈ y_i⟨H⟩/√(R MUV). Oscillation probabilities are parametrized by the six standard oscillation parameters plus R and the lightest Dirac-mass parameter.

Following the earlier DDG model, a lifetime-threshold estimate assumes states heavier than the mass corresponding to lifetime t have already decayed. This yields characteristic mass evolution m_l ∝ t^(-2/7); the visible decay width scales cubically with mass. High-redshift normalization is then propagated to the local universe.

Mirror periods, Picard–Fuchs equations, analytic continuation and direct integration of holomorphic anomaly equations determine free energies. Modified constant maps, conifold gaps and refined Castelnuovo vanishing constrain holomorphic ambiguities.

The mathematical construction uses Fourier–Mukai equivalences, moduli of stable one-dimensional sheaves and perverse sheaves of vanishing cycles. Geometric examples use signed Euler characteristics, with intersection cohomology when curve moduli are singular.

Analyze the one-modulus charge family p^0=0, p^1=N, q_0=−y²N, q_1=0 at large y. Relate horizon moduli to distance, evaluate the ADM mass at fixed asymptotic moduli, and vary quantized charges to estimate neighboring attractor spacing.

Solve algebraic attractor equations for horizon periods and insert them into the central-charge entropy formula. Repeat with a corrected prepotential to express leading and subleading geometric data through charges and BPS degeneracies.

Relate the modified elliptic genus of the K3 MSW string to four-dimensional D4-D2-D0 BPS indices. For wrapping number r=1, use Zμ=η^(-24)Φμ and Noether–Lefschetz coefficients to infer selected non-BPS string excitations in five dimensions.

Compute gauge kinetic matrices from triple intersections and analyze their leading asymptotic rank. Compare the inverse kinetic quadratic form with the species cutoff; a vanishing coupling in Planck units alone does not establish the required weak coupling.

Evaluate the Repulsive Force Conjecture using the inverse gauge kinetic matrix and scalar metric, including gravitational and scalar-mediated attraction. The heterotic excitation mass includes both string tension and a charge-dependent Coulomb-branch shift.
Evaluate the D6 world-volume action to obtain the hard string-core tension and estimate thickness from the local string length, whose largest boundary-space size occurs at the horizon.

Construct charged straight-string modes by matching a near-source flat-space Maxwell–Chern–Simons solution to a flat intermediate region and then to linearized curved-space meson modes at large distance.

Expand the D8 action to quadratic order, giving five-dimensional Maxwell–Chern–Simons theory. Treat the D6 boundary as a magnetic source in the Bianchi identity, then solve using radial eigenfunctions and modified Bessel functions; the zero mode is logarithmic and represents the ALP.

Insert EFT amplitudes and numerical bootstrap amplitudes into the Bell expressions. Random MES-setting statistics are generated in Mathematica by randomizing four angular variables and maximizing over four others; the pion study also averages I3 over energy.

Normalize the outgoing scattering amplitudes and evaluate CGLMP joint probabilities. For the leading two-amplitude photon state, the chosen settings give I = 2√2(Φ1Φ2* + Φ2Φ1*)/(|Φ1|² + |Φ2|²), with Φ1 = g2 s² + higher orders and Φ2 = f2(s²+t²+u²) + higher orders.

Study isotropic and nonisotropic charge limits to diagnose large/small entropy and the validity of a classical-volume proxy. Compare the resulting species scale with Kaluza–Klein scaling as a consistency check, replacing the classical volume by a Kähler-potential-based quantum volume when necessary.

Use special geometry, electric/magnetic attractor equations and Wald entropy at the horizon. Homogeneity rewrites the entropy as a Legendre transform of the functional ℱ=4π Im F, with electric potentials φΛ and ∂ℱ/∂φΛ=−qΛ.

Encode the supersymmetric curvature correction through a background chiral multiplet A and a generalized prepotential F(X,A)=Σg Fg(X)A^g. The known correction is proportional to c2i Im zi Tr R∧*R, with c2i determined by the Calabi–Yau second Chern class.

Dimensional reduction of the Einstein–Hilbert action, Weyl rescalings, canonical normalization of the logarithmic volume field, and cosmological time redefinitions relate Kasner metrics to Einstein-frame kination.

For an exponential scalar potential plus radiation, the authors construct an autonomous system in normalized kinetic/potential variables, use N=log a, and classify critical points by linear stability.

Analytically continue the type IIA prepotential using Jonquière’s trilogarithm identity. Across a collapsing nop class, the reported updates are κ′abc=κabc−n⁰C CaCbCc and c′a=ca+2n⁰C Ca, with the effective charge reassigned from C to −C.

First scan the dual of an inner effective-divisor cone built from inherited and min-face divisors. If necessary, reconstruct T_hyp and scan its lattice sites. Charges are bounded by d=v_g·q≤d_cutoff, with v_g strictly inside K.

Compute genus-zero GV invariants using mirror symmetry/CYTools, approximate the infinity cone, identify nilpotent extremal rays strictly outside it, and adjoin chambers across flops and stable Weyl reflections.

The static, spherically symmetric saddle solves Euclidean Einstein equations with effective fluid stress Tab = (λ/N)γab and zero energy density. A D-dimensional TOV equation determines the lapse; horizon conditions require N = 0 and dN/dl = 1.

The action is evaluated using Einstein–Hilbert and Gibbons–Hawking–York terms and, separately, Einstein–Hilbert Noether-charge identities. The authors also obtain a Smarr relation and κδAV = κkδV − VξδΛ, where k is boundary extrinsic-curvature trace and Vξ the Killing volume.

A constrained-instanton path integral introduces λ(ϕ) on a contour parallel to the imaginary axis, imposing a delta-function constraint on the volume of every time slice. Its contour is deformed through a real saddle value; the constraint term vanishes on shell.

At the parent attractor point, compare its mass with sums of constituent central-charge magnitudes. Impose charge conservation and BPS/anti-BPS sign conditions, then maximize the ratio separately in allowed charge domains.

Solve ∂aV_BH=0, distinguish BPS solutions by ∇aZ=0, and examine the Hessian. The imported ansatz t̂ᵃ=ipᵃz yields general BPS/non-BPS solutions; special intersection tensors allow additional solutions without proportionality to pᵃ.

Varies the metric f(R) action and rewrites the vacuum equations using the matrix M=α^−1g and a parametrization of the two-dimensional metric block. A restrictive relation between α and fR makes two reduced field equations identities.

Introduces auxiliary functions w, Ψ=lnψ and W=lnw, integrates the off-diagonal metric equations, and substitutes g=dw/dφ in the residual equation. General branches are represented in quadratures; selected integration constants and exponents yield elementary functions.

Reduces the remaining PDEs to ODEs using either a travelling-wave-type combination or a logarithmic variable. The logarithmic variable is ln[(t²−z²)/4] in the nonstationary case and ln[(z²+ρ²)/4] in the spatial case.

For T=0, tune the torsional Weierstrass ansatz to introduce an isolated codimension-two (4,6) point, then blow it up to acquire a tensor multiplet. Birational invariance preserves Mordell–Weil torsion under blowup; the preceding tuning may enhance, but is claimed not to reduce, the 1-form sector.

For the Z7 exclusion, impose center neutrality of matter using the SU(7)^3 quotient embeddings (1,2,3). Matter multiplicities force each supporting curve to have genus at least one; the authors then show that the residual discriminant class is not effective.

Restrict Y3 to a generic rational fiber f of B2→P1. Adjunction identifies the restricted elliptic surface Y2 as K3; restriction of sections is asserted to be injective and to preserve torsion orders, allowing use of the known K3 torsion classification.

Estimate nucleation using the Hartle–Hawking wavefunction and a saddle approximation. Perform mass and charge integrations approximately by first fitting entropy linearly in the mass coordinate at fixed charge, then also fitting the endpoint entropies linearly in charge.

Represent fixed mass and charge through delta-function constraints and Lagrange multipliers integrated parallel to the imaginary axis. Generic conically singular RNdS geometries are interpreted as stationary points of this modified, constrained action.

Evaluate two Euclidean caps cut along a zero-extrinsic-curvature slice. Separate regular and conical curvature contributions, include the charge-fixing Maxwell boundary term, and use the generalized Smarr relation. The boundary contribution localizes on the horizons and cancels the remaining β-dependent term.

Import an inflationary entanglement-entropy density generated by cubic curvature interactions, then multiply by the physical Hubble volume 4π/(3H³). The paper invokes global purity to identify the entanglement entropies of the two momentum sectors.

Use von Neumann entropy bounds and the Page-curve behavior of large random pure bipartite states to motivate a possible bounded entropy evolution. The cosmological application is presented as requiring further justification.

Estimate crossover times by equating the growing entanglement estimate with π/H². Re-entry and purification during radiation and matter domination are compressed into a factor f rather than calculated dynamically.

Use modular flows to generate an alternative entanglement-wedge algebra. Modular flow describes internal evolution; half-sided modular inclusions generate horizon-crossing translations in the reviewed eternal-black-hole example.

Construct state-dependent representations by GNS completion of products of centered single-trace operators. Leading correlation-function factorization produces a Gaussian generalized free field description.

Relate Minkowski, Rindler and interval/complement oscillators through basis changes, conformal maps and analytic continuation. Locate bulk wedges by finding where coefficients of complementary oscillators vanish.

Sample four late-time parameters, Ωbh², Ωch², θ and τ, together with inflationary parameters and Ne. The potential normalization determines the scalar amplitude; ns and r are derived from model spectra rather than independently imposed slow-roll formulas.

ModeChord directly solves perturbation equations for primordial scalar and tensor spectra. CAMB evolves these through transfer functions; CosmoMC, connected through PolyChord, compares angular spectra with the CMB likelihoods.

Represent uncertain reheating through generalized reheating: Ne = NIRH − (1 − 3wre)Nre/4. Sampling Ne therefore incorporates a restricted family of post-inflationary histories instead of fixing a single horizon-exit e-fold count.

Compute anomaly condensates by integrating chiral gravitational-wave modes up to an ultraviolet cutoff, then use the axion equation and stress tensor to obtain a nearly constant axion velocity and an effective running-vacuum energy density. These calculations are summarized from cited studies.

Absorb the antisymmetric-tensor kinetic contribution into a torsionful connection, implement its modified Bianchi identity with an axionic Lagrange multiplier, and use the total-derivative form of the gravitational Chern–Simons density to obtain derivative coupling to its topological current.

Review a two-axion potential with condensate-induced linear terms and nonperturbative periodic modulations, and semi-analytic right-handed-neutrino decay calculations in an axial background. The temperature-dependent leptogenesis calculation uses Padé approximants.

Use SVT decomposition, Fourier transformation, and quadratic perturbation actions to inspect kinetic coefficients. Solve the metric tensor equation through conformal-time rescaling, Bessel/Hankel functions, and subhorizon/superhorizon asymptotics.

Vary the action for background Einstein equations, linearize homogeneous deviations around de Sitter, and inspect the evolution matrix eigenvalues. Rewrite slow-roll evolution in e-fold time and integrate numerically using fourth-order Runge–Kutta.
A separate reviewed consistency test uplifts tensor gravitational waves on the bubble to AdS5 and compares their induced second-order backreaction with a direct four-dimensional Einstein calculation.

The reviewed propagator calculation uses Lorenz gauge, transverse Fourier transformation, piecewise modified Bessel functions K2 and I2, horizon regularity, shell matching, and brane bending to recover the tensor response and its trace structure.

The reviewed local analysis combines Gauss–Codazzi curvature relations with thin-shell junction conditions, including bulk mass and string-cloud sources, to obtain the induced four-dimensional Einstein equations.

Reduce on a round S² with metric ansatz ds4²=(Φ0/Φ)ds2²+Φ²dΩ2² and a purely electric gauge field. This gives a consistent spherical truncation; the Maxwell field is retained rather than eliminated because charge may vary.

Compute renormalized on-shell actions. The AdS2 treatment uses boundary counterterms and a double Legendre transform for the gauge sector; the flat treatment adds Gibbons–Hawking, dilaton, and Mann–Marolf terms, the latter implementing background subtraction.

Split coincident horizons using a small parameter λ, perform near-horizon decoupling limits, and match the four-dimensional response to linear fluctuations Φ=Φ0+λY, g=ḡ+λh, and gauge-field perturbations, allowing arbitrary δQ initially.

Noether-current fluxes determine source matching constants. Exterior solutions are translated into PPN parameters; numerical interior searches are supplemented by a weak-gravity, slowly varying expansion about the source centre.

Explicit dimensional reduction tracks metric and volume factors in bulk kinetic terms and covariant, gauge-invariant brane interactions. Four-dimensional dualization uses a Bianchi-identity Lagrange multiplier and Gaussian integration over the three-form field strength.

Gronwall's lemma converts the differential upper bound ȧ/a≤H0 into an exponential bound on a(tf)/a(ti). Logarithmic endpoint assumptions then yield TCC-form inequalities; an integrable envelope is used to seek a uniform bound on an infinite interval.

The argument invokes Picard existence/uniqueness for continuation of bounded scale-factor solutions and an imported geometric completeness theorem involving integrable lapse-gradient and extrinsic-curvature norms. Integrating a positive lower bound on H supplies the proposed complementary bound on a.
Analytical unoriented gradient orbits are compared graphically with numerical IR-optimal cosmological orbits. IR-optimal means the initial velocity is chosen as −grad_G V at the initial position.
The imported dynamical renormalization/uniformization framework replaces first-order IR orbit analysis by negative gradient flow of the classical effective potential V with respect to G.

Principal canonical coordinates diagonalize the critical-point Hessian. Quadratic potential expansions and asymptotic hyperbolic metrics give integrable local orbit equations; at critical ends the implicit solutions involve the lower incomplete gamma function of order two.

A semiclassical saddle for a general four-form interaction W(X) produces a Legendre-transformed scalar potential. The paper also uses unwarped dimensional reduction to four-dimensional Einstein frame and canonical normalization to extract brane-matter couplings.

Constrained path-integral dualization treats the three-form field strength as independent and imposes its Bianchi identity with a scalar Lagrange multiplier. Integrating different variables gives equivalent scalar and two-form descriptions; adding a three-form extends the construction to a massive scalar.

Improve a nonconserved current by subtracting a locally defined Chern-Simons form. When the nonconservation term is locally exact and integrates to zero on trivial topology, this gives a Page charge. Dress its operator with defect-localized topological degrees of freedom to restore gauge invariance and topological behavior on more general manifolds.

Construct rational defects by higher half-space gauging finite magnetic subgroups with discrete torsion and boundary TQFTs. A seven-dimensional analogue of a fractional quantum Hall TQFT cancels the F_4∧F_4 anomaly; Type II examples instead use mixed gauging. An alternative method introduces compact Stueckelberg-like fields directly on the defect.

Fixed-t dispersion relations follow from contour deformation, crossing symmetry, and high-energy boundedness. Subtracting low-energy discontinuities gives improved positivity bounds. In gravity the UV dispersive contribution is matched to the divergent graviton t-channel pole before taking t→0 from below.

The explicit amplitude analyses use pole residues, gamma-function asymptotics, and dispersive sums or branch-cut integrals. The one-loop argument uses Feynman parameters, loop-momentum power counting, light-particle threshold cuts, and a formal higher-spin exchange sum expressed through a Lerch function.

The authors truncate the background equations, solve a cubic equation in H², expand at small dimensionless potential, and differentiate the resulting relations to compare kinematic slow roll with potential slow-roll parameters.
Metric variation and Bianchi identities supply the modified gravitational and matter continuity equations, which are specialized to the homogeneous cosmological background.

Methods include power counting of gauge-allowed symmetry-breaking operators, dimensional estimates of induced fermion loops, expansion of the axion potential, and mixed-anomaly matching. The supplement obtains QCD and electroweak Chern-Simons couplings proportional to (NDW a/Fa)g²/(32π²).

The authors solve cubic and mixed gravitational U(1)g anomaly constraints together with Yukawa charge constraints. Their restricted charge ansatz gives the two fermion sets the same charge multiset in different orders. Replicating a smaller coprime solution p times yields k=pk', l=pl', and NDW=p.

Match constant-equation-of-state reheating dilution to a thermal radiation density and entropy-conserving expansion. Apply an integral bound on present-day PGW energy density from excess radiation, obtaining a reheating-temperature lower bound and illustrative detector-spectrum comparisons.

Use modified Friedmann and scalar equations, the Hubble slow-roll hierarchy, and analytic integration of the exit-to-end e-fold interval. Integrate the scalar trajectory from the Hubble evolution to reconstruct V(ϕ) parametrically, and scan parameters against P-ACT-LB confidence regions.

The plane-wave review relates the two mode bases through Bogoliubov transformations. Near-horizon mode inner products produce gamma-function coefficients; their products give number-operator expectation values in the Kruskal vacuum and the thermal spectrum.

Frequency smearing constructs localized packet creation operators and their number operators. Cutting the Kruskal-frequency integral at ΛΩ and changing variables using the exponential blueshift converts the result into truncated integrals over packet densities. Gaussian examples yield complementary-error-function profiles.

Reviews Mandelstam–Tamm and geometric quantum speed limits, including Wigner–Yanase information for unitary evolution; uses a relative-purity bound and Lindbladian evolution for the Markovian open-system extension.

Uses spherical-harmonic generators and their Poisson algebra, operational clustering of the density matrix, and lowest-order invariant generator traces. Variational functionals are interpreted as quantum constructions rather than quantizations of classical actions.

The review describes Kaluza–Klein compactification from ten-dimensional string theory or eleven-dimensional M-theory/supergravity to four-dimensional low-energy theories. The resulting effective theory depends on the compactification choice; no explicit compactification calculation is supplied here.

It reviews applying conjectured restrictions on scalar potentials to single-field inflation observables r and n_s. The reported phenomenological application is explicitly said to have been questioned.

A nondegenerate pairing on polyhomogeneous solutions tracks gluing obstructions through a finite-dimensional characteristic system. Its solvability is equivalent to orthogonality to the substitute cokernel; iteration removes exponentially small errors.
Min-max arguments bound low spectral counts. The G2 application combines a contraction mapping with quadratic Sobolev estimates for the nonlinear remainder.
Fourier separation and meromorphic resolvents split cylinder solutions into regular Fourier multipliers and explicit Heaviside convolutions associated with real poles.

Extended c=9 N=2 character formulas, half-integral spectral flow and theta-function identities rewrite one-loop contributions as derivatives of Ramond characters. Differentiation in the charge chemical potential inserts the fermion-number operator.

The proposed evaluation route uses open topological strings and holomorphic anomaly equations, with Chern–Simons theory or matrix-model techniques where applicable. Explicit compactification examples remain a stated next step.

The calculation starts from an imported string-field-theory expression for |W_Γ|. Its K₀ factor exponentiates regulated annulus and Möbius integrals with measure dt/(2t); a universal-zero-mode subtraction regulates the infrared divergence.

Expand higher-dimensional fields in warped-Laplacian eigenmodes to obtain KK masses; match the flux scalar potential to N=1 supergravity to normalize W; expand the D-brane DBI action to identify gauge couplings controlling gaugino condensation.

Track metric determinants, inverse metrics and form-field contractions through ten- and four-dimensional Weyl transformations. Dimensionally reduce and canonically normalize fields to distinguish physical masses from mixed-frame scale parameters.
LATTICEEASY computes the preheat-field dispersion, inserted into ΔU=½M²Ψ̃⟨Ψ̃i²⟩ and Utot=U+ΔU. The stated lattice has 128³ points and rescaled edge length L=40, with L=m̃Lphys and m̃=10⁻⁶mP.

Transforms from Jordan to Einstein frame using Ω²=1+ξϕ² and a canonical field χ; U=V0/Ω⁴. The inverse field map ϕ(χ) is approximated by a fitted rational function with numerator and denominator of degree ten.

A modified LATTICEEASY implementation uses a Green-function method for tensor perturbations sourced by transverse-traceless stress. Spectra with and without ΔU are compared at the same H=5.5×10⁻⁹MP; late spectra are reported to stabilize.

Eliminate the magnitude of Φ̇ through the constraint, retaining its sign, and solve equations linear in the Hubble-parameter derivatives. Construct phase portraits for H and h; separately integrate the zeroth-order equations analytically with zero or constant potential.

Vary the first multitrace contribution α′³c4,1[Tr(Ṡ⁴)]², initially treating S as unconstrained and then projecting the variation using S²=1. Include its contributions to directional evolution equations and the lapse constraint through third order in α′.

Expand a d-dimensional QFT into a (d+1)-dimensional SymTFT slab with topological and dynamical boundaries. Bulk operators form the Drinfeld center; a boundary Lagrangian algebra specifies which operators terminate. Gauging changes the topological boundary while preserving the bulk SymTFT.

Compute defect correlator phases in 3d and 5d Dijkgraaf–Witten theories using discrete cochain path integrals. Linking numbers are expressed through intersections of operators and Seifert surfaces; magnetic operators receive worldvolume TQFT decorations to ensure gauge invariance.

Expands Λ/M_P^4 in powers of M_{3/2}/M_P, subsequently restricting to even powers. In the single-tower Dark Dimension setting, the leading power satisfies k = 4n; the authors interpret this through a leading nonzero supertrace contribution.

Studies four-dimensional N = 1 F-term supergravity with constant superpotential and a corrected tree-level no-scale Kähler potential. Compares potential and gravitino scalings with KK masses after converting string units to four-dimensional Planck units.

Counts light KK species to estimate the quantum gravity cutoff. For one tower, Λ_QG = m1^(1/3) M_P^(2/3), giving approximately 10^9 GeV; for two towers, multiplies their species counts before solving for the cutoff.

Set ε1(φf)=1 and determine φi from the e-fold integral: N=∫[φi,φf](ξ″/ξ′)dφ for Gauss-Bonnet, or N=∫[φf,φi]κ²V/(αV′)dφ for Chern-Simons. Evaluate observables and conjectural diagnostics at first horizon crossing.

Vary the actions with respect to metric and scalar, then apply slow roll. In constrained Gauss-Bonnet gravity, ξ̈=Hξ̇ gives φ̇≈Hξ′/ξ″; the scalar continuity equation is used to reconstruct V from the chosen ξ.

Use perturbative beta functions for general quartic single-trace superpotential couplings, with leading contributions controlled by the superpotential and γΦ. Solve the fixed-point equations for the nearest-neighbor chain and check positivity of each squared coupling.

Count scalar and fermion constituents of low-dimension R-neutral trace operators. Shift every species index by two to multiply charge by nine without changing constituent counts, then compare the resulting upper bound on Δmin(9q0) with conjectured superadditivity and the unitarity bound.
Hamilton–Jacobi reconstruction treats H(ϕ) as primary, uses Ḣ=ϕ̇H′ to obtain first-order field evolution, and reconstructs V. Inflationary evolution is parametrized by ε₁=−Ḣ/H² and ε₂=ε̇₁/(Hε₁).

Reheating is constrained through expansion matching and entropy conservation. An imported integral bound on the present PGW energy density, using the quoted ΔN_eff≤0.17, supplies an additional lower reheating-temperature bound.

Using their adopted constant-c_s prescription, the authors compare the horizon-crossing slow-roll expressions n_s=1−(2ε₁+ε₂) and r=16c_sε₁ with observational contours. These comparisons are conditional on that prescription and perturbative control. P_s supplies a normalization fixing ξ, rather than treating every dimensional parameter as independently free.
Reconstruct scalar kinetic and potential contributions through the density–pressure correspondence, then plot the scalar field, potential, and quantities labeled as refined swampland criteria.

Use graphical redshift evolution to examine energy densities, dark-energy pressure and equation of state, total-fluid energy conditions, and a sound-speed stability diagnostic. The supplied discussion does not establish a full perturbative stability result.

Integrate component continuity equations and reconstruct dark-energy density, pressure, and equation of state from geometrical quantities. Close the background system with a prescribed Hubble function, an approach the authors call a model-independent parametrization scheme.

Place the Euclidean theory on an infinite cylinder of circumference R and write E(R)=−πc(mR)/(6R). Obtain stress components from E/R and dE/dR, then isolate the r² bulk term in the UV expansion of c(r), where r=mR.

Use thermodynamic Bethe ansatz equations with kernels G=−i∂θ log S. Relate the massive bulk term to the leading large-|θ| kernel coefficient; for massless flows use coupled left/right pseudoenergies and match the corresponding kernel asymptotics.

Apply barrier-peak WKB quantization, including displayed higher-order corrections, at a near-event-horizon potential maximum r0. Estimate the fundamental imaginary frequency and compare its decay rate with horizon surface gravities.
Separate the charged Klein–Gordon equation using spherical harmonics and e^(−iωt), introduce the tortoise coordinate dx=dr/f, and reduce radial dynamics to a Schrödinger-like equation.

Starts from a Planck-suppressed Kähler coupling between the modulus and PQ-charged fields, integrates out heavy PQ fields, and expands in the axion superfield to obtain component interactions and two-body decay widths. A two-field gravity-safe PQ construction supplies an effective λPQ.

Uses the authors' nine-component coupled Boltzmann framework, including number and energy evolution, annihilation, decay, injection, inverse decay, and relativistic lifetime dilation. Coherent modes have vanishing annihilation and pressure; the coherent axion requires its temperature-dependent mass term.

Numerical implementation uses C++/Boost special functions and Odeint's Rosenbrock 4 solver for stiff annihilation terms. Modified IsaReD supplies temperature-dependent neutralino coannihilation rates; scans vary modulus and PQ parameters.

Decompose duality groups into amalgamated products, apply Mayer–Vietoris and prime localization, and shear twisted tangential structures into twisted Spin bordism. The main computations use the Adams spectral sequence; the Spin-BD6 contribution uses Atiyah–Hirzebruch.

Use A(1)-module cohomology, Ext-module actions, naturality, Margolis' theorem and May–Milgram/Bockstein relations to constrain differentials. Explicit lens spaces, bundles and eta invariants detect generators and resolve hidden extensions; the E-infinity page alone supplies only an associated graded group.

Estimate one-loop kinetic metrics by summing tower states below the species cut-off. For the chosen linear masses and couplings, the dominant fermion metric scales as N0^3 ≃ (Mp/m0)^2; heavier independent towers give g_i ∼ (ΛQG/m0^(i))^3.

Canonically normalise diagonal kinetic metrics: Yijk = Sijk(g_i g_j g_k)^(-1/2). Order-one UV couplings thereby acquire tower-dependent suppression factors; generation-dependent factors are used to construct qualitative fermion mass textures.

Construct angular bases from products of scalar, vector, and tensor spherical harmonics, including mixed-sphere rank-two tensors. Split parity sectors and use gauge transformations to simplify Maxwell and metric perturbations.

Reduce radial equations to Rosen–Morse potentials V=a+b tanh(dx)+c/cosh²(dx), transform y=[1+tanh(dx)]/2, and solve through hypergeometric functions. Boundary asymptotics and Gamma-function poles select frequencies; Dirac separation uses tensor products of Pauli matrices and spin-weighted harmonics.

Constructs α-vacua as squeezed-state-type excitations of conjugate QNM vacua, obtains the Euclidean limit α*→−∞, traces southern modes, and maps bulk operator products to boundary correlators using BPZ bra–ket identifications.

Uses the global Klein–Gordon pairing and its matrix NAB to define mode operators, commutators, and a linear bulk field reconstruction formula. The explicit matrix is not needed for the main construction.

Organizes scalar solutions into SO(4,1) highest/lowest-weight quasinormal and antiquasinormal towers and their descendants. Linear combinations give four real mode families with support excluding one static patch.

Solve coupled Boltzmann number-density equations for χ and a using thermally averaged 2→2 rates, ALP decay/inverse-decay rates, Hubble dilution, and detailed balance. Scan hidden-sector and connector couplings to identify production regimes and relic-density contours.

For decoupled freeze-out, evolve hidden-sector energy density as a third equation to obtain its temperature T′ and evaluate hidden-sector reaction rates at that temperature. The resulting three coupled differential equations are described as stiff and solved numerically.
Recalculate model-specific exclusions from SLAC electron beam dumps, stellar and supernova energy loss, and rare kaon and B-meson channels, including invisible and dilepton ALP decays.

Estimates conversion using dfdecay/dt=κM*max/[Mpeak(z)tcrit]. Integrated conversion between first halo collapse and z=20 is limited to 2.62%, importing a historical 2σ decaying-dark-matter bound as an approximate recast rather than performing a new cosmological likelihood analysis.

Combines Bose-enhanced gravitational and self-interaction condensation rates through τ=τself τgr/(τself+τgr). A phenomenological growth model uses initially exponential growth followed by M*∝t^(1/α), varying α from 1 to 5 to represent uncertainty.

Models the initial isocurvature spectrum as cutoff white noise, with a general power-law extension. Press–Schechter spherical collapse and a sharp k filter estimate halo populations; the calculation replaces the distribution with characteristic Mpeak, growing as (1+z)^−2 for white noise.

Anomaly descent and inflow are applied to a string regularized by a radial bump function: 1+ρ vanishes at the core and ρ vanishes outside it. This converts the worldsheet matching problem to consistent gauge anomalies; allowed local counterterms implement reduction of discrete anomaly coefficients modulo n.

The authors solve fermion Dirac equations in vortex backgrounds and match the resulting chiral zero modes to bulk inflow. Background higher-form gauge fields and auxiliary five-dimensional inflow actions diagnose higher-group mixing and 't Hooft anomalies.

Linear stability analysis supplies sufficient slow-roll conditions. Curvature spectra use Green functions for temperature-independent dissipation; temperature-dependent cases generally require numerical coupled inflaton, radiation and metric perturbations. The review chooses zero-shear gauge for numerical stability.

Integrating out environment fields using the in-in closed-time-path or influence-functional formalism produces stochastic dynamics. Noise and dissipation obey a fluctuation-dissipation relation; adiabatic localization yields a Markovian equation and a dissipation coefficient expressed through retarded self-energies.

Special Kähler geometry, BPS attractor equations and comparison of scalar potentials establish the dictionary. Matching with hypermultiplets invokes h_uv k^u_Λ k^v_Σ=P^x_Λ P^x_Σ for the stated electric abelian gauging with constant quaternionic Killing vectors.

Wrapped-brane sourcing and flux jumps construct the microscopic correspondence. Buscher T-duality maps IIB NS5-brane domain walls sourcing H3 into IIA Kaluza–Klein monopole domain walls sourcing geometric flux.

One-loop messenger matching generates mixing and scalar–photon interactions. The scalar-dependent electromagnetic coupling enters the two-loop plasma free energy. Scalar evolution is treated using a linearized high-temperature equation, power-law solutions and WKB reasoning.

The replicated model's one-loop Coleman–Weinberg potential is expanded to all orders in messenger parameters r,r′ using two methods: Fourier transformation and cosine sum rules. The displayed complete expansion assumes N>4.

Boltzmann equations estimate freeze-in from transverse resonant γ→A′ conversion below the electron-pair threshold and inverse decay e−e+→A′ above it. The inverse-decay collision integral uses Maxwell–Boltzmann distributions and a low-temperature Bessel-function approximation.

AdS solutions are constructed by shooting from a smooth neck and tuning initial scalar values to match asymptotic falloffs. In IIB, u−v∼r^−6 and 4u+v∼r^−8 log r. The appendix describes objective-function optimization and increasing-cutoff extrapolation using known asymptotics.

The reviewed GS construction uses O(d)-symmetric geometries and timelike target-space geodesics with c<0. Regularity requires an available geodesic longer than the geometry's required length. For decoupled pairs in flat space, Σ_iβ_i^−2>(d−1)/[2(d−2)]. This geodesic criterion does not directly apply when a scalar potential is present.

Derive the Rarita–Schwinger consistency condition by gamma contraction and divergence of its eigenvalue equation. Construct vector-spinors from a transverse-traceless Lichnerowicz tensor and the Einstein-squashed Killing spinor; for the squashing singlet the derivative and algebraic constructions are proportional.

Construct invariant scalar, tensor, form and spinor eigenmodes explicitly. For operators admitting continuous deformation, count singlets by decomposing round-sphere SO(8) representations under Sp(1) × Sp(2). This counting argument is explicitly unavailable for Rarita–Schwinger modes.

RG improvement replaces classical couplings by running ones and identifies k with a physical infrared scale. Bianchi consistency can constrain this identification; improvement of the action introduces derivative terms absent from field-equation improvement.
Refinements reviewed include iterative self-consistency, improvement of scalar Zakhary–McIntosh invariants, and inverse-propagator decoupling conditions combining competing physical infrared scales.

Functional RG through the Wetterich equation, approximated by derivative, vertex or curvature truncations. Momentum-dependent curvature form factors enter the effective action; quantum geometries should solve δΓ0/δg=0.

Test the framework through spectral sums, Wick contractions, special-function representations, conformal-block expansions and sphere free-energy asymptotics. For finite-state Euclidean quantum mechanics, finite spectral sums give observables in Rexp; the free-particle and oscillator examples also generate Rexp.

Use first-order formulas, graphs of functions, finite Boolean operations and projections to define structures. Apply imported monotonicity and cell-decomposition results to translate o-minimality into finiteness and regularity statements.

Sum Galactic and redshift-integrated extragalactic primary and annihilation emission, integrating to zmax=100. Isotropic bounds require the predicted flux not to exceed any data point by more than 2σ; the SMM line is treated with approximately 7% energy resolution.

Compute Hawking particle spectra with species-dependent greybody factors, using supplied literature factors said to agree with BlackHawk. Integrate positron emission above me and convert the rate to line luminosity through the photon yield fline.

Target flux scales as fline fPBH(dNe/dt)/(4πM) times the integrated dark-matter column density. Galactic limits use either total measured emission or the amplitude extracted with an NFW spatial template.

Spherical-harmonic expansion and a Gaussian WDW/WKB ansatz reduce mode evolution to Riccati equations, then linear equations solved with associated Legendre functions. Analytic continuation and turning-point matching connect Euclidean branches to the expanding Lorentzian branch.

Use Gaussian mode probabilities with σ_n²=1/[2 Re(R_n)], then sum n²σ_n² for the field variance. Horizon smoothing regulates the ultraviolet sum, implemented through a window or cutoff n_*∼exp(Ht); the resulting distribution estimates late-time inflating volume.

Leading semiclassical instanton comparison using P_nuc ∝ exp(−|S_E|), so the smallest action magnitude dominates. Near the transition, a domain-wall ansatz and illustrative quartic potential supplement the negative-mode argument.
Inflation ends by the prescription ε₁=1. The integral N=∫H dφ/φ̇ then determines the horizon-crossing field value, where observables are evaluated.
Variation with respect to metric and scalar gives background equations; transverse-traceless tensor perturbations are Fourier decomposed into circular polarizations.
Adopts a cited WKB propagation treatment, h_M=e^(−D)h_GR, giving an energy-spectrum factor e^(−2D). D<0 enhances the spectrum; a blue tensor tilt can additionally enhance high frequencies.

Construct four-point amplitudes from derivative contact terms, quartic potential contacts, and cubic-potential exchange in the s, t and u channels. Compare total amplitudes between coordinate bases rather than requiring their separate kinetic and potential contributions to coincide.

Express interactions through curvature tensors and derivatives of the potential. Real-field potential derivatives are symmetrized covariant derivatives; the KNC potential expansion uses ordered complex derivatives and specified combinations. Alternatively, transform the potential explicitly and use ordinary partial derivatives.

Flatten the field-space metric at a chosen background using vielbeins, then rotate to diagonalize the mass matrix. Expand in RNC or use holomorphic transformations to KNC; both eliminate cubic derivative interactions, simplifying tree-level amplitude calculations.

Mixed holographic boundary conditions make the boundary metric and scalar source dynamical. Holographic renormalization supplies finite stress tensors, scalar expectation values and anomaly-corrected Ward identities.

Boundary Friedmann and inflaton equations are evolved together with the bulk. Initialization is implicit because the scalar expectation value depends on H′ and QFT energy depends on ϕ″, producing a sixth-order polynomial constraint.

A characteristic formulation in generalized Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates reduces the bulk evolution to nested radial ODEs. Near-boundary subtraction, pseudospectral grids and radial gauge shifts support numerical evolution.

Four-point correlators are decomposed into intermediate Liouville momenta and Virasoro blocks. Zamolodchikov recursion generates truncated elliptic-nome expansions; crossing symmetry reduces the moduli integral to a finite domain.

The three-punctured sphere reduces to a product of Liouville three-point coefficients. The four-punctured sphere requires integrating the product of the two Liouville four-point functions over its complex modulus.

For numerical integration with the modulus integrated first, channel counterterms subtract regulator-induced power divergences. A small disk around z=0 is treated analytically with a next-to-leading-order block expansion; its exterior is integrated numerically.

Construct an autonomous system using e-fold time, dimensionless kinetic, potential, curvature, Gauss–Bonnet and fluid variables. Classify fixed points through eigenvalues, and impose an additional compatibility equation inherited from the tensor-speed constraint.

Approximate the background by R²-dominated quasi-de Sitter evolution, H(t)=HI−M²t/6. Evaluate five evolution indices and the scalar/tensor spectra at first horizon crossing, using numerical examples to compare with the Planck constraints cited by the paper.

Impose ξ̈=Hξ̇ so that the tensor-speed correction vanishes. Combine this constraint with the axion equation to obtain algebraic expressions for φ̇ and the index ε2; the linear coupling is treated separately because the general expression divides by ξ″.

The five local-comparison posterior samples are combined with equal weighting. A separate WISE–COSMOS high-redshift comparison, said to require no BH bias corrections, returns k=2.96 with bounds +1.65 and −1.46.

A windowed Monte Carlo samples progenitor masses and metallicities, estimates stellar lifetimes and remnant masses, applies coupled growth, and sums present BH mass density. Windows target ≤1% Poisson errors in their least probable bins.

Sample realizations include reported uncertainties and measurement/selection-bias corrections. BH masses are shifted to z=0 for trial k, then an Epps–Singleton test compares high-redshift and local distributions.

Scan fixed cutoff scales Λ and compare EFT against GR with Gaussian-noise likelihoods and nested sampling implemented in parallel bilby. The reported joint statistic multiplies the three per-event Bayes factors.

Use the stationary-phase frequency-domain waveform and decompose its phase into GR, neutron-star tidal and dimension-6 pieces. The displayed correction contains terms proportional to vf^10 and vf^12 inside the overall phase prefactor, with suppression by (GMΛ)^4.

Retain the dimension-6 basis LD6=α1I1+α2(I1−2I2), apart from operators stated not to contribute to the relevant Ricci-flat solutions. Imported potential and radiation corrections provide the waveform modification.
Treat formation as an nrad→n scattering process with transition time ∼R. An allowed energy window ΔE≲Esat/Ssat and cosmological cooling give β∼1/(Ssat HR); the leading estimate is p∼β when β≪1.

Compare radiation and composite entropy at matched radius and sufficient energy: Srad=N∗(RT)^3 and Erad=N∗T^4R^3. Estimate quantum production through entropy suppression compensated by final-state microstate degeneracy.

The scalar-spectrum prescription is imported from earlier warm G-inflation work: stochastic Langevin fluctuations sourced by thermal noise, with fluctuation–dissipation input and coupled inflaton–radiation growth for temperature-dependent dissipation.

PBH abundances use Press–Schechter density-tail probabilities and smoothed density variance. Scalar-induced GWs use a second-order scalar-to-tensor convolution, its late-time radiation-era kernel, and redshifting to the present energy-density spectrum.

Slow-roll background parameterization and integrated Q_G evolution determine parameters using the end condition ε_H=1, 50 or 60 remaining e-folds, and the normalization Δ_R²(k_P)=2.1×10⁻⁹ at k_P=0.05 Mpc⁻¹. Spectral-index predictions are compared with the paper's Planck bounds.

Use Weyl transformations between Jordan and Einstein frames and to remove leading source-density couplings; derive point-particle forces through variational identities; apply a WKB expansion to axion-coupled Maxwell equations.

Expand metric, scalars, matter and field equations in PPN potentials. Solve successively for Newtonian fields, spatial metric, mixed metric components, and fourth-order fields; potential identities turn the differential equations into algebraic equations for expansion coefficients.

For the quantum case, add proper-time dissipation to a scalar wave equation, estimate turning/reflection positions using WKB, and integrate the entropy of two bosonic polarizations over transverse momentum and cavity overtones with measure A d^2k⊥/(2π)^2.
For the classical case, use an approximate WKB QNM spectrum, assign energy ω̃=|ω|, sum Boltzmann weights into Z, and evaluate canonical entropy S=ln Z−β∂βln Z at β=βH.

Scalar evolution uses the homogeneous Klein-Gordon equation; generalized-dark-matter fluid modeling specifies w(a), rest-frame sound speed c_s²(k,a) and anisotropic stress. Linear continuity/Euler evolution connects EDE perturbations to the Weyl potential, acoustic driving and early integrated Sachs-Wolfe contributions.

Bayesian MCMC constraints are compared with profile likelihoods, which minimize χ² over other parameters at fixed parameter of interest. The stated tension metric is Q_DMAP=√[χ²_min(with SH0ES)−χ²_min(without SH0ES)], interpreted in Gaussian σ units; its Gaussian equivalence does not justify Gaussian treatment of arbitrary marginalized posteriors.

The authors reconstruct F(R̄) from Jordan-frame equations using a(t)=tⁿ, then test potential inequalities. The restricted parameter slice is analyzed analytically; independent λ and μ require numerical compatibility regions. Constant H is treated separately.
An auxiliary-field reformulation and conformal transformation of only the spatial three-metric introduce φ̄=(2/3)ln F′ and φ=αφ̄. Choosing μ=λ−1/3 removes the mixed metric–scalar derivative term.

Relate integral monodromies to compact rotations by conjugation; use an SL(2)^4/Z2 subgroup to obtain explicit allowed angles. Narain lattices supply complementary constructions, including examples outside this subgroup ansatz.

Construct sector/projector partition functions using theta functions, invariant-lattice sums and Poisson resummation. Extract low oscillator states by q-expansion, cancel orbifold charges with circle momentum, and determine twisted multiplicities using fixed-point factors and invariant-lattice volume.

Localized explosions are modeled using coupled shock-radius and pressure equations adapted from supernova remnants. Integration stops when the bubble can no longer ionize swept gas; subsequent cooling and recombination determine a volume-averaged electron fraction.

Coupled baryon-temperature and effective three-level-atom equations include hydrogen and singly ionized helium, Compton and expansion cooling, collisional ionization/excitation cooling, and axion heating. RECFAST expressions are used with photon-ionization terms evaluated at Tγ rather than Tb when their equality fails.

Axion-star abundances and energy-injection histories are imported from the authors' previous extended Press–Schechter and Monte Carlo merger-tree calculation. Explosions are assigned to plasma-delayed supercritical stars or rapidly growing stars produced by major mergers of comparable masses.

Derives gauge and axion kinetic matrices from dimensional reduction. In Type IIB, the five-form self-duality constraint is implemented before eliminating dual field strengths; wrapped-cycle volume bounds identify BPS particle masses.

Kaluza-Klein reduction expands ten-dimensional forms in harmonic forms on the internal manifold; integration over the Calabi-Yau and Weyl rescaling determine four-dimensional kinetic terms and brane actions.

Uses periods of the holomorphic three-form, projective special Kähler geometry, symplectic charge vectors and the central-charge relation. Explicit checks employ a cubic prepotential through the stated mirror-symmetry identification.

RNS graviton two-point amplitudes are evaluated on the torus, annulus, Möbius strip and Klein bottle, extracting the order-p² coefficient. Momentum conservation is relaxed to p1 + p2 = ξ with ξ² = 0, while masslessness, transversality, tracelessness and p1·p2 = 0 are retained.

Jacobi-theta identities and spin-structure sums reorganize amplitudes into characters of the extended N = 2 algebra and supersymmetric indices. Boundary and unoriented correlators use the doubling/image method. The torus receives only the odd–odd spin-structure contribution.

Weyl rescaling with exp(-2Φ̃4) = exp(-2Φ4) + δE, together with one-loop holomorphic-coordinate redefinitions, relates string-frame amplitudes to the Einstein-frame moduli metric. The small-curve application estimates changes using counts of low-lying states rather than a complete internal spectrum.

Starting at k = 0 and real Z, an ordinary differential equation determines superpotentials with V = 0 along a flat direction. Combining the two branches and restoring stabilization produces the vacuum potential, scalar masses and supersymmetry-breaking sector.

For selected N and v, numerical equations V′I = V″I = 0 locate k0,z0 with v < z0 < 1. The inflationary displacement δk = k−k0 and mass scale m are then constrained using the curvature amplitude and required e-folds, while the spectral index constrains the horizon-exit position.

A semi-analytic treatment expands VI cubically about z0 and approximates the canonical-normalization factor by J0, neglecting specified products of the small linear and quadratic coefficients. Slow-roll integrals and observables are compared by the author with numerical results.

Adapt Abelianisation on the Hopf fibration and Euclidean N=2 supersymmetric localization to nontrivial flat background connections and complex levels. Gauge fixing reduces the path integral to Cartan integrals with Ray-Singer torsion factors.

Use a DHS-inspired reconstruction of determinants from meromorphic mass dependence, quasi-normal modes and horizon regularity. Schwinger parameters organize weight sums into Wilson-loop traces; the initial spectral product carries an explicit erratum.
Expand the localized integrand at large s, perform Gaussian moments, and evaluate the remaining α integral by residues at nonzero multiples of 2π. Residue sums become polylogarithms.

Compute flavor transformations as outer automorphisms of the Narain space group; use their representations to constrain superpotential and Kähler invariants. Dedekind-eta modular forms generate common mass-matrix structures, expanded near symmetry-enhanced alignments.

Fit historical GUT-scale charged-fermion inputs and NuFITv5.1 lepton-mixing information by numerical χ² minimization with lmfit, then explore minima with emcee MCMC. The seven-parameter lepton fit has two reported best-fit regions.

Uses a static spherical metric parametrized by A=e^(2h)f and B=f^−1, together with Einstein equations and a radial mass function f=1−2m/r, to motivate cancellation of the collapsing shell's gravitational mass.

Compare the redshift trend quoted from a referenced black-hole/stellar-mass analysis with the direction implied by growth with scale factor. For gravastars, sum matter and compact-object density-pressure contributions and discuss whether negative pressure could dominate.

Reduce the bulk action using Maurer–Cartan forms and include expanded non-Abelian Dirac–Born–Infeld and Wess–Zumino source actions. Couplings to dual RR potentials determine open-string corrections to bulk field strengths, which then enter the reduced potential.

Construct flux/embedding-tensor dictionaries for ζ_M, ξ_M and antisymmetric f_MNP, impose their quadratic constraints, and parameterize the scalar coset in compactification variables. Compare the resulting quadratic embedding-tensor potential with the bulk-plus-source potential.

Solve f(r+)=0 for M, use S=πr+²/G and T=f′(r+)/4π, and rewrite M as a function of S,Q,C,b,α. Thermodynamic conjugates are then obtained through partial derivatives.

Real-time smearing is explained using the iε boundary value of OPE singularities and repeated integration by parts. Holomorphy from energy positivity and power-law bounds permit finite smeared operators even when purely spatial smearing fails.

Authors reduce warped Einstein–dilaton–form equations to bulk ordinary differential equations, impose delta-source jump conditions, and compare warp factors, dilaton and curvature in proper-distance coordinates.

BF constructions separate transverse coordinate dependence and use polar coordinates for the ETW defect. Type A closure additionally includes the original codimension-one source, which reaches the singularity.

Embedding-tensor quadratic constraints characterize consistent gaugings and their possible maximal-supergravity embeddings. In the seven-chiral sector, the authors use a Kähler potential and superpotential and report that the analytic vacua satisfy DI W = 0.

Symmetry-invariant truncations guarantee that their extrema are extrema of the full scalar potential. The authors calculate the full half-maximal bosonic and fermionic mass spectra, apply standard AdS4/CFT3 mass–dimension relations, and organize operators into superconformal multiplets.
Functional differentiation of relative entropy and coordinate transformation laws are used to identify metrics, connected and 1PI vertices, connection symbols, non-metricity and curvature.
