Hölder's inequality establishes convexity of W; the Legendre transform Γ[Φ]=sup_J(J·Φ−W[J]) supplies expectation coordinates and the field equation δΓ/δΦ=J.

Set fermion supersymmetry variations to zero, apply very special geometry identities, and split vector fields into a chosen gauging direction and orthogonal directions. Kinetic-matrix positivity relates vacuum energy to physical gravitino couplings.

For maximal supergravity, use the scalar-dressed embedding tensor, or T-tensor, and USp(8) tensor identities to rewrite the scalar potential in terms of Killing vectors and gravitino gauging matrices.

Differentiate V(Phi), calculate potential slow-roll quantities and observables, and eliminate Phi to plot swampland constants against n_s and r. The comparisons use Planck 2018 and model inputs attributed to reference [105].

Represent the exponential nonlocal operator using an auxiliary diffusion coordinate rho>=0, with F(0,t)=F(t) and F(rho,±infinity)=F(±infinity). Choose F=Phi=alpha^n exp(beta rho)t^(nq); the authors then obtain a claimed exact H(t) and reconstruct V(t) through the scalar equation.
Gauge-invariant cosmological perturbation theory and Fourier-mode quantization; field-space covariant tangent/normal projections analyse multi-field trajectories and turning.

Dimensional reduction to N=1 supergravity specified by a Kähler potential and superpotential; minimization of moduli potentials incorporating fluxes, perturbative corrections and nonperturbative effects.

The FLRW continuity equation is combined with density dilution ρ̄∝a^−3 to recover the zero-pressure condition for stable objects of negligible self-gravity. A momentum-conserving source term is then introduced to model cosmologically varying mass.

A Newtonian hydrostatic-equilibrium and binding-energy example illustrates nonzero internal mean pressure for self-gravitating objects. For strong self-gravity, the author invokes Birkhoff's theorem and the Schwarzschild exterior rather than extending the von Laue condition.

Transform to horizon-regular Bondi–Sachs coordinates to evaluate tidal Weyl components. For charged holes, AdS₂ and spherical-harmonic decomposition converts the linearized equations into an algebraic condition on γ.

First correct the symmetric near-horizon background, then expand stationary axisymmetric deformations as ερ^γQᵢ(x). The Kerr problem reduces to two second-order equations; zeroth-order Sturm–Liouville eigenfunctions use Legendre polynomials, followed by perturbation theory for γ.

Canonical quantisation imposes Hamiltonian and momentum constraints as operator equations. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation admits a conserved Klein–Gordon-type current; ordinary probability density cannot automatically be identified with |Ψ|².

Saddles are constructed using South Pole series expansions, slow-roll matching and numerical optimisation of complex initial data to reach real final fields. Anisotropic examples use a higher-dimensional Newton algorithm.

Gauge fixing with ghost fields and BRS symmetry reduces the lapse functional integral to an ordinary integral. Picard–Lefschetz theory deforms suitable specified contours into convergent steepest-descent thimbles.
Use the warped Kähler metric, GVW superpotential and F-term potential to estimate conifold and gravitino masses, uplift-induced stabilization shifts, and inequalities preventing runaway.

Estimate throat and bulk KK scales from the ten-dimensional metric and scalar Laplacian; obtain uplift from DBI plus Chern–Simons terms. Their shared spacetime redshift explains the fourth-root scaling.

Build finite-volume completeness relations from overlap equations for primary-mode and Virasoro-descendant states, accounting for singular vectors through the Kac determinant. Insert these relations between operators to construct four-point conformal contributions.

In D=2 combine direct contour integration, holomorphic/antiholomorphic factorization and algebraic state construction. The author extends integer-weight contour results using Ward recursions, unitarity boundary conditions and finite-degree polynomial dependence at fixed excitation levels.

Derive conformal-generator actions on spatially integrated modes, impose Ward identities, reduce correlators using conservation laws, and solve resulting differential equations by series and recursion. In D=3 spherical-harmonic products are organized with Wigner 3j symbols.

Scan nearby parameters while maintaining the scalar amplitude near the Planck normalization. Supplement numerical tensor spectra with a heuristic vacuum-plus-sourced estimate using imported asymptotic formulas, including F²∼exp(3.6mQ); this estimate is explicitly only for orders of magnitude.

Expand to quadratic order, canonically normalize coupled scalar and tensor modes, impose Bunch-Davies initial states, and numerically solve matrix mode equations separately for each tensor chirality and wavenumber.
Numerically evolve the background using e-fold time dN=Hdt. A slow-roll effective potential for Q supplies approximate stationary solutions and guides the choice of a positive global minimum.

Find complex zeros of transcendental spectral functions and classify pole residues numerically. Large-|ν| harmonic-number asymptotics give logarithmic approximations reducible to X log X = −a; flat-space analysis uses Lambert-function branches.

Linearize bulk and boundary Einstein equations, use Fefferman–Graham expansions, and determine the nonlocal tensor response by solving bulk radial equations with interior conditions. The inverse graviton propagator combines a local gravitational operator with the CFT stress-tensor two-point function.

Compare exact tower mass scalings in Planck units and maximize their minimum over moduli space. Define ζi=−∂i log m; use the imported convex-hull analysis containing a radius-1/√(d−2) ball to identify a decreasing tower in every nonperiodic direction.

Use canonical field distances, duality fundamental domains, and endpoint-distance arguments to obtain path bounds. In the Calabi–Yau examples, follow tower masses across flop phases on the F=1 vector-multiplet slice.

Numerically solve three coupled Friedmann-like equations for a(t), b(t) and the moduli-flow contraction, scanning the bulk cosmological constant. Separately impose ḃ=0 and eliminate the moduli contraction to obtain an analytic class.

Organize axions into a symplectic vector and use Calabi–Yau periods and special Kähler geometry. Vanishing hyperino supersymmetry variations is used to reduce the bulk stress tensor to an expression involving complex-structure moduli.
Gauging introduces a background fermionic (p+1)-form Ψ with δψ=ϵ and δΨ=dϵ. Higher-dimensional extensions using Ψ−dψ organize the proposed anomaly/inflow description.

Equations of motion give conserved tensor-spinor currents whose Hodge duals define on-shell topological generators. Stokes' theorem, distributional Poincaré duals and path-integral field shifts yield linking-number actions; a quadratic distributional self-term is handled by a local counterterm.

Introduce dual potentials through first-order duality equations exchanging Bianchi identities and equations of motion. The Ehlers example explicitly uses a parent action with a Lagrange multiplier to replace a three-dimensional vector by a scalar.

Perform toroidal Kaluza-Klein reduction with a triangular vielbein and γ=−1/(D−2), obtaining the lower-dimensional Einstein frame directly. Decompose higher-dimensional forms into lower-degree forms with coupled gauge transformations and nonlinear Bianchi identities.

Describe scalars by G/K representatives, decompose V⁻¹∂μV=Qμ+Pμ, and construct a sigma model from Pμ. Triangular gauge makes geometric shifts explicit and realizes hidden transformations through compensating local K rotations.

Use orientifold, T-duality and S-duality relations to access the heterotic description. For computation, T-dualize the IIB configuration along x³ and uplift to eleven dimensions, translating much brane data into geometry and G-flux.

Define normalized metric expectation values through a path integral around the interacting Minkowski minimum, inserting a non-unitary displacement operator D(σ). The total action includes kinetic, interaction, ghost and gauge-fixing terms.

Replace the full field content by three representative scalar degrees of freedom. Analyze shifted-vacuum nodal diagrams, Borel-resum their Gevrey growth using a principal-value prescription, sum over interaction couplings, and use a cosine Fourier transform to specify the metric displacement profile.

Compute linear vector perturbations in radial gauge A_u=0, with spatial momentum along x and infalling horizon conditions. Obtain retarded current correlators from the quadratic on-shell boundary action, then apply the stated Kubo prescription.

Use WKB at large frequency and a small-frequency/momentum expansion for hydrodynamic transport. The appendix proves tensor identities using Ricci/Weyl decomposition and mutually orthogonal projectors on the time, radial and planar directions.

For Einsteinian Cubic Gravity, derive a reduced second-order background equation and solve it numerically by shooting from a regular horizon expansion to the asymptotic region. Causality is examined through a Schrödinger-form vector equation with potential V=1/(BS).

Separate massive-mode contributions from short-distance massless-scalar contributions. Expanding Λs around a scalar vev generates scalar-curvature vertices; scalar exchange produces higher-dimension operators smeared over radius Λs⁻¹. Comparing their coefficients motivates the gradient bound.

Use the integrated holomorphic anomaly equation for F1, expressed through the Kähler potential, metric determinant and holomorphic ambiguity. Scale saxions toward boundaries and retain logarithmic subleading terms to estimate corrections to the species-scale slope.

Analyze asymptotic global geodesics as boosts acting on the charge lattice. Null boost lines identify candidate light charges; BPS completeness and the mild WGC are then used to argue that lattice points on these lines support BPS states.

Use dimensional reduction and gauge/scalar kinetic-term matching to relate 9d moduli to type I′ parameters and 8-brane positions. Imported rank-one 5d SCFT Coulomb-branch classification constrains allowed internal geometries through small-instanton probes.

Estimate GW emission using the quadrupole formula, scaling-regime wall energy and cosmological redshift with entropy conservation. Adopt simulation-based efficiency and spectral behavior, and compare predicted amplitudes with the detector sensitivities used in the paper.

Estimate annihilation by equating wall tension pressure σ/t to the bias Vbias, giving H(Tann) ≃ Vbias/(2σ). For approximately spherical closed walls, estimate the enclosed mass from surface and false-vacuum volume contributions, and use compactness p(t) = 2M(t)/(t MP²) ≃ 1 as the PBH-formation criterion.

Parameterize the remaining network energy density after annihilation begins by ρwall(T)/ρwall(Tann) ≃ (T/Tann)^α. Infer possible α values from published simulated wall-area decay times, then redshift the estimated PBH density to obtain fPBH.

Linearize R² with an auxiliary scalar and eliminate its algebraic constraint after Weyl transformation. For R² plus symmetric Ricci squared, introduce an auxiliary tensor and use a disformal transformation with a slow-roll expansion.

Weyl transformation ḡμν=A(φ)gμν followed by canonical field redefinition gives U=V/A². The canonicalization contains an additional (3/2)(A,φ)² contribution in metric gravity, absent in Palatini; the review encodes this with κ=1 and κ=0 respectively.

For non-minimal derivative coupling, use a disformal metric transformation, expand the Einstein-frame action at small X under slow roll, and compute observables directly through the non-canonical field when canonicalization cannot be integrated analytically.

Even self-dual charge lattices of signature (1,17), assumed moduli-induced similarity transformations, and increasing boosts of Γ1,1 are used to identify BPS towers and alternative ten-dimensional limits.

Supersymmetry-variation cancellation fixes the dilaton dependence of BPS string tension. Broken-supercharge Clifford algebras and Spin(8) triality determine winding-string ground-state representations.

Postinflationary durations are calculated by matching a pivot mode across cosmological eras and using adiabatic temperature relations. Tensor propagation is treated with a WKB approximation, h=e^(−D)h_GR, and transfer functions for the gravitational-wave spectrum.

Impose ξ̈=Hξ̇ and approximate φ̇≃Hξ′/ξ″. The scalar continuity equation then reconstructs either V from a first-order equation or ξ from a second-order equation, leaving only one freely designated scalar function.
Use analytical inequalities, numerical approximations, contour plots, and intersections of allowed regions. N=60 is adopted to reduce parameter spaces and is used for the displayed model constraints.
Determine φend from εV(φend)=1; obtain φi using N≈(κ²/β)∫[φend,φi](V/V′)dφ; evaluate spectral quantities at φi and impose observational inequalities.

Reduce the spherical ansatz to one-dimensional radial dynamics with a Hamiltonian constraint. Evaluate the potential term on the unperturbed near-core solution to determine relevance, and solve the critical case with a logarithmic profile.

Analyze gauged axion shifts through dual BF couplings and gauge-invariant dressed operators. A wrapped-D3 example identifies the string-emission number with a flux integral and symplectic pairing; STU charge choices then test asymptotic exploration subject to this obstruction.

Use a two-dimensional entropy function on constant-modulus AdS₂×S² configurations, extremizing over both radii and the scalars to obtain the effective attractor potential. A four-dimensional entropy-function derivation is also supplied.

Use continuous norm-preserving group representations and restriction to real slices to distinguish states that can be transformed between slices from those confined to a slice. The representation conclusions are summarized from the author's earlier work.

Test whether mixed states admit a ray-compatible T operation by comparing a superposition with its common-phase multiple. Separately analyze tensor-product matrix elements and invoke Wigner's theorem to argue against T symmetry of the interacting sectors.

Expand fields in creation and annihilation operators, assign different unitary/antiunitary discrete transformations to the sectors, and follow a schematic absorption vertex under T. This is an illustrative operator argument rather than a calculated scattering rate.

Review logarithmic corrections from an R4-induced localised Einstein–Hilbert vertex exchanging KK gravitons with D7 stacks through two transverse dimensions. The amplitude discussion uses an orbifold limit before its CY interpretation.

Organise scalar potentials through master formulae using intersection numbers, Euler characteristic and two-cycle variables; present large-volume expansions, three-field numerical extrema and reported Hessian eigenvalues.
Use the N=1 F-term potential with Kähler-covariant derivatives, first imposing DS W0=DU W0=0, then adding corrections that break the Kähler-sector no-scale cancellation.

Construct O(4)-symmetric Euclidean bounces with locally constant vacuum scalars. Compute Γ/Vol∼exp(−B/ℏ), where B is the instanton action minus the complete parent-vacuum action, then analyse curvature limits and model-specific flux jumps.
Vary the bulk and boundary actions, impose Israel junction conditions and Δχi=−Qi, and classify membrane geometries using X=4Mpl^4Δk²/T² and nonnegative tension.

For the quintic, scan D-brane charges and numerically minimize |Z| = |e^(K/2)q·Π| near previously observed crossings. The procedure uses local minimization rather than integrating the attractor flow, and includes a prescribed monodromy adjustment across the relevant argument branch.

Sample hypersurface points using the ambient Fubini–Study measure, approximate Ricci-flat metrics with neural networks, and expand eigenfunctions in a finite basis pulled back from ambient Laplacian modes. Benchmark these approximations against the exact torus spectrum.

Compute torus periods through Picard–Fuchs hypergeometric solutions or a Weierstrass transformation and Klein j-function. Compare the crossing condition with integer quadratic equations defining nontrivial torus endomorphisms.

Construct su-related dispersive sum rules, then impose st crossing using thrice-subtracted relations. Subtraction of the crossed expressions cancels EFT terms proportional to t^n with n≥3, leaving improved sum rules usable near t=−Λ².

Estimate coefficient sizes by normalizing dispersion relations with Λ and assigning schematic spectral-function scalings. Improved sum rules can contain mutually cancelling contributions, so the prescription surveys available rules and retains the smallest inferred scaling.

Expand helicity amplitudes in Wigner d-functions and use the generalized optical theorem. Integrating sum rules against optimized functions of p=√(−t) converts UV positivity into semidefinite conditions. Independent spectral channels are organized into matrices with basis {00,+0,++,+−}, separated by intermediate-state parity and even/odd spin.

Use anomaly descent and inflow, requiring I4+I4_inflow=0. CS/WZW duality motivates boundary-string degrees of freedom supplying opposite-sign currents; a gravitational CS term accommodates unequal left/right central charges.
Vary boundary canonical charges and use Dirac brackets to obtain asymptotic current algebras; extend GR boundary conditions by permitting both gauge components to vary.

Define an elastic-helicity contour quantity A(t) from the sum of two crossed helicity amplitudes divided by (s−2m²+t/2)^3. Evaluate it within the EFT, then deform the contour to UV cuts using analyticity, Hermitian analyticity and asymptotic boundedness.

A numerical feasibility iteration decreases m²/M² until no dRGT parameter point satisfies the finite-t bounds. A separate all-derivative argument strips little-group factors, expands partial waves, and uses positive moments, crossing null constraints and Hankel-matrix inequalities.

Positivity of scattering norms for superpositions bounds inelastic matrix elements of M†M by elastic ones. Combining this with high-energy approximate crossing bounds finite-t dispersive quantities using forward elastic quantities. Crossing errors are bounded by calculable forward EFT terms rather than unknown UV amplitudes.

One-loop KK vacuum energies are expressed as logarithmic determinants and proper-time heat-kernel integrals. Torus sums can be evaluated using Jacobi theta functions; dimensional regularization isolates ultraviolet poles.

Higher-dimensional short-distance heat-kernel expansions identify local counterterms schematically proportional to m⁶, m⁴R, m²R² and R³. Orbifolds additionally require counterterms localized at orbifold points.

Sum Euclidean gravitational weights over configurations. For Kerr–dS, evaluate bulk Einstein–Hilbert, Gibbons–Hawking–York and counterterm contributions; derive free energy, entropy and average energy from Z using thermodynamic derivatives.

Separate the tensor metric as gμν(x,θ)=χ(θ)gμν⁽⁴⁾(x), solve the resulting curvature/profile equations, and impose circle periodicity. Dimensional reduction then supplies the effective action and configuration-dependent Planck scale.

Assess stabilization through canonically normalized scalar spectra, using ZAB=e^(K/2)DADB W, the inverse Kähler metric, fermion masses and μ²±λ=(m3/2±mλ)². The authors report evaluating the unreduced field system as a numerical consistency check.

First choose tadpole-contributing fluxes and solve the limiting equations for vi=ti/t0. Select a target dilaton inside the stretched CS cone, tune the remaining fluxes toward Q′target, then numerically solve the polynomial LCS system. Singular M additionally imposes flux consistency constraints.

Use mirror triple intersections and polynomial prepotential data at LCS. The imported IIB1 flux restriction fA⁰=hA⁰=hAⁱ=0 gives a quadratic polynomial superpotential, linear axion equations MB=−L, and decoupled nonlinear saxion equations involving Q′ and the generalized inverse M⁺.

Reduce the mass relation using degree-one homogeneity, vanishing identical-object force, and an imported expression relating scalar charge to charge derivatives of the mass. These ingredients produce a first-order nonlinear ODE.

Numerically integrate the reduced equation once per coupling instead of repeatedly shooting for individual black holes. Midpoint geometry and local curvature diagnose binding-energy signs; Appendix B uses stationary-point analysis for a perturbative positivity proof.

The higher-derivative hypermultiplet ansatz contains 33 coefficients. The authors organize independent supersymmetry variations into a reported system of 58 equations for 35 parameters, first treating structures independent of H and the dilaton gradient, then examining the remaining structures.

An on-shell Noether procedure requires δ0L1 to vanish modulo the lowest-order field equations Eφ. Remaining terms f(ε,φ)Eφ determine first-order transformation corrections δ1φ=−f(ε,φ), rather than requiring an off-shell hypermultiplet formulation.

Linear-H variations subsequently require additional hyperino bilinears LH; dilaton-gradient variations require no new terms after imposing the coefficient solution.

Kneser–Nishiyama construction: choose the rank-six complement T0 = TS⊥ inside E8, then enumerate primitive embeddings of T0 into the 24 positive-definite Niemeier lattices. Orthogonal complements determine the possible frame lattices, with the geometric sign reversal tracked through discriminant forms.

Algorithm 2 answers only whether a rootless complement exists. It recursively discards pairs of extension vectors that leave any ambient root orthogonal; surviving pairs must still satisfy the conditions defining T0. It handles difficult cases without enumerating every frame lattice.

Algorithm 1 embeds the root part of T0 through simple-root identifications, extends by vectors of prescribed norms and inner products, checks primitivity, and computes the rank of roots orthogonal to T0. This yields minimum non-Abelian rank when the scan is exhaustive.

Use symmetry and conservation to reconstruct the stress tensor from its trace as an inverse-radius expansion. The p = 4 term is omitted because it is treated as electric-charge renormalisation; recovering the full tensor is conditional on the imposed symmetry assumptions.

Combine the imported trace-anomaly extremality shift with corrections from local R², RF², F⁴, and derivative-of-F operators. Matter-loop backreaction is interpreted through its relation to corrections of 1PI gravitational amplitudes.

Expand the corrected trace equation in powers of lP/L. Curvature-independent, R, and F² terms are absorbed into renormalised cosmological constant, Newton constant, and gauge coupling before studying the leading remaining corrections.

The four-point loop is treated by Feynman parametrization, a momentum shift, Wick rotation and an approximation for small external momentum relative to Λ. The running-coupling check differentiates the vertex counterterm with respect to an auxiliary UV cutoff and then identifies that cutoff with μ.

One-loop two- and four-point amplitudes are combined with mass, field and interaction counterterms defined through a non-local bare-field rescaling. Illustrative conditions include on-shell two-point subtraction and the φ4 vertex condition at s=4m², t=u=0.

Euler–Maclaurin summation separates integral, endpoint and Bernoulli-remainder contributions. Authors compare cylindrical and spherical hard cutoffs with Gaussian smooth cutoffs, numerically evaluate remainders, and fit polynomial coefficients where analytic integration is unavailable.

KK Fourier expansion and fluctuation determinants relate the 5D and 4D potentials. The conventional calculation is reviewed using the Schwinger identity, Poisson resummation, Jacobi theta functions and polylogarithms.

Reviews anomaly calculations through particle production and Landau levels, triangle diagrams and Fujikawa’s regulated measure. An anomalous quark rephasing transfers the axion–gluon coupling into the quark mass matrix for matching to the chiral Lagrangian.

Differential forms, exterior derivatives, Hodge duals, integral cohomology and patchwise gauge connections organize flux quantization. A Bogomol’nyi rewriting relates Euclidean Yang–Mills action bounds to self-duality and instanton number.

Dimensional reduction produces f²=1/(2πR e₅²) and converts a five-dimensional A∧tr(G∧G) Chern–Simons term into the axion–gluon coupling. Charged Kaluza–Klein spectra illustrate monodromy: a 2π axion shift permutes modes while preserving the full spectrum.

The comment compares variation of the conformal factor with arbitrary spacetime dependence against variation restricted to δa(η). It identifies how taking both a and δa outside the spatial integral converts a local source equation into an averaged homogeneous equation.

An algebraic scalar-field action with an external source supplies a toy counterexample: solve the unrestricted stationarity equation and compare it with the equation obtained after imposing a homogeneous ansatz and homogeneous variations. This tests the variational step without constructing a black-hole spacetime.

Use supersymmetric vacuum conditions and special-geometry identities to rewrite vacuum energy through gravitino charges and gauge couplings; project onto a canonically normalized unbroken gauge direction before applying the WGC.

Match bulk anomaly inflow to string-worldsheet anomalies using Chern–Weil descent, tangent/normal-bundle decomposition, and matrix-rank bounds. The review explicitly sketches rather than fully derives the rank analysis.

Engineering dimensions define a dimensionless g. The paper uses a Callan–Symanzik-type equation for vacuum energy and integrates a quoted one-loop beta function to discuss positive and negative coupling trajectories.

A constant-field saddle evaluates Z≈exp[−βV V(ϕ₀)] with V′(ϕ₀)=0. Expanding the sinh-Gordon cosh potential through quartic order motivates comparison with λϕ⁴; an analytic continuation in m² is then invoked.

Dilaton Fourier modes diagnose radius-dependent KK scales. A probe D4 DBI action supplies its position-field metric; field redefinitions expose an H²×R³ metric for the reduced interpolation sector, permitting explicit geodesic estimates.

Dimensional reduction gives V=G^{IJ}P_I P_J−4P². The authors solve ∂P=0 analytically/numerically using five equal deformation moduli σ and a sixth τ. Physical scalar masses use the kinetic-metric-normalized Hessian, rather than raw Hessian eigenvalues.

The main computational method is the Adams spectral sequence: at 2, a change-of-rings result reduces the E2 page to Ext over A(2); odd primes are treated directly. Module actions, naturality, and manifold characteristic numbers constrain differentials and extensions.

Ordinary vector-bundle shearing fails: Lemma 2.2 excludes spin bundles realizing λ=c1+c2 or λ=2c on the respective gauge classifying spaces. The replacement uses generalized MTString-module Thom spectra classified by maps to BGL1(MTString).

Three nonlinearly coupled ODEs for the background inflaton, its first-order perturbation and the gauge-invariant Bardeen potential are solved numerically in Mathematica 12. Their solutions supply mode-dependent spectra, e-folds, tilts, running and Hubble parameter.

The inflationary scale M is fixed through COBE/Planck scalar-amplitude normalization. Comparisons use Planck-2018 public chains and marginalized contours generated with GetDist; these are the paper's historical observational benchmarks.

The previously developed DHE formalism evaluates successive horizon crossings using k = aH. Treating these crossings as a continuous, one-to-one time–momentum mapping gives dk/dt = ä and converts time evolution into k-space equations; a nonzero ä is required.

Near the critical barrier, the action is expanded about an inflection point, the slowly varying DBI kinetic term is expanded to quadratic order in velocity, and the potential is retained through cubic order. Published variational perturbation expansion results for a cubic oscillator supply the complex ground-state energy.

The one-loop calculation uses the second-variation Sturm–Liouville operator, removes its translation zero mode and regularizes the determinant ratio through spectral zeta functions and an imported contour-deformation method. The relevant bounce sector has one negative mode and one zero eigenvalue.

The bubble radius is treated as a Euclidean quantum-mechanical coordinate with a noncanonical DBI action. The corrected radius-dependent energy gain involves a hypergeometric function; bounce profiles and the action relative to the trivial configuration are evaluated numerically.

Supporting geodesic analysis separates the null Hamiltonian using conserved momenta and a Carter-like constant. Critical light rings correspond to double roots of a cubic radial polynomial; general separated trajectories can be expressed through elliptic integrals.

The quantum Seiberg–Witten approach computes periods in an instanton expansion. Angular regularity requires aA = nA + 1/2 with nA = ℓ/2; outgoing radial modes use a − aD = nr. The charged-mode calculations focus on the lowest overtone nr = 0.

Scalar modes are obtained by separating the six-dimensional wave equation. Matched near-cap hypergeometric and far-region Bessel solutions provide initial frequency estimates; numerical integration imposes cap regularity and outgoing infinity behavior through a vanishing matching Wronskian.
Coset harmonic analysis uses the master equation ĎaY=−TaY and −Ď²=Cg−Ch. A universal Laplacian and Casimir expressions for Weyl-tensor action streamline the operator equations.

Explicit modes are generated from scalar harmonics using differential operators and Sp1 projectors. Diagonalisation, divergences, scalar products and vanishing norms determine transverse spectra and exceptional low-label irreps; two-form construction requires symmetrised second derivatives.

The Killing spinor decomposes gamma-traceless vector-spinors as 48→7⊕14⊕27 under G2. Transversality relations and previously analysed tensor equations yield squared spin-3/2 eigenvalues; supersymmetry supplies linear-operator sign information.

Dimensional reduction and Weyl rescaling to Einstein frame; extremization of the universal volume/dilaton potential; comparison with traced, integrated higher-dimensional Einstein and dilaton equations.

Integrated Bianchi identities impose tadpoles. Internal Laplacian eigenvalues estimate KK masses; holographic scalar dimensions diagnose scale separation once operators dual to KK modes are identified.

Keep particle charge fixed when obtaining Eq. (2.18), without a near-horizon expansion. Numerically compare λ² with κ² while scanning charge at fixed angular momentum or angular momentum at fixed charge, and map the equilibrium solutions to radial intervals.

Use the charged-particle Lagrangian and Hamiltonian to obtain radial evolution in coordinate time t, impose the massive four-velocity normalization, and linearize the flow in (r, πr) about πr = dπr/dt = 0. Eigenvalues of the radial Jacobian provide the local instability exponent.

First-order dualization imposes F = dA with a λ multiplier and integrates out F; the quadratic example is Gaussian. The general map uses λ = ∂L̂/∂F and L(λ) = L̂(F)−λF. Because A is cyclic in the bulk, the author identifies this as a Routhian transformation. Boundary terms are retained for the variational principle.

Semiclassical Euclidean bounce analysis glues locally maximally symmetric geometries across a charged thin membrane using flux and Israel junction conditions. Instanton branches are classified by ζout,in = ±1. Nucleation rates use Γ ∼ exp(−Sbounce), with Sbounce = Sinstanton−Sparent.

A minisuperspace Wheeler–DeWitt treatment and leading WKB approximation neglect scalar kinetic energy to discuss nucleation weights: exp(−24π²/V) for tunneling and exp(+24π²/V) for no-boundary boundary conditions. These are imported semiclassical formulas.

Homogeneous parameter scans are combined with saddle-point estimates of unstable-mode growth and fragmentation time. Modified CosmoLattice simulations include curvature in background evolution and are compared with the fragmentation estimate.

Oscillation averaging replaces the rapidly oscillating scalar by an effective fluid. Expansion reduces its amplitude until wavg>−1/3 permits turnaround; contraction increases amplitude until wavg<−1/3 permits a bounce when curvature balances positive energy.

The applied correction is BBH=Bs,vir+BL⋆+Bm,vir(Hα), with adopted components −0.3, −0.5 and −0.3 dex. The authors include these negative shifts as a conservative test. They omit positive biases, stating that including those would lower inferred k.

The local fit has central relation log10 MBH=8.66+1.32 log10(M⋆/10^11 M⊙). Combining it with cosmological growth gives μi(k)=1.32 log10 M⋆,i−k log10(1+zi)−5.86. A product Gaussian likelihood compares μi with bias-corrected logarithmic BH masses; BH mass error, converted stellar-mass error and intrinsic scatter are added in quadrature.

Selection requires z>4, broad-Hα significance >5σ, E(B−V)<0.1, images without unresolved point sources or disks, and SFR below an adopted redshift-dependent main-sequence criterion. The adopted main-sequence scatter is 0.1 dex for 0<z≤6 and 0.4 dex for 6<z≤10.

Diagonalize the propagation Hamiltonian and use the oscillation-averaged probability P̄αβ=Σi|U^m_αi|²|U^m_βi|², justified by rapid oscillations and limited energy resolution. Map source fractions to Earth using fα,⊕=ΣβP̄βαfβ,S.

Sum source-dependent Yukawa potentials at the detection point. The cosmological contribution includes expansion and a redshift average weighted by comoving volume and source density following the star formation rate.

Bayesian marginalization uses P(V)=∫dϑ L(⟨f⊕⟩)π(ϑ)π(V), with a uniform-in-V prior over 10^-24–10^-16 eV. Mixing priors retain θ23–δCP correlations; future DUNE/HK precision is simulated with GLoBES and combined with JUNO projections.

The authors sum Yukawa potentials from point-source Moon and Sun models and continuous Earth, Galactic and cosmological distributions. The cosmological contribution is evaluated locally at redshift zero; detailed source integrations are adopted from earlier work rather than reproduced here.

Mean spectra without statistical fluctuations enter a Poissonian χ² with normalization pulls. The likelihood is profiled over sin²θ23, δCP, |Δm²31| and mass ordering. Joint sensitivity sums the two experiments' likelihoods before profiling; potential bounds are mapped to mass-dependent effective-coupling bounds.

Oscillation probabilities are obtained by numerical Hamiltonian diagonalization. GLoBES with the snu library supplies reconstructed-energy event spectra, efficiencies and backgrounds for electron appearance and muon disappearance in both beam modes; wrong-sign events are added to the signal.

Expand fields along torsion differential-cohomology classes of S³/Γ and integrate using its linking pairing LΓ. The middle term gives LΓ∫M5 G3∪g2; integrating over g2 is interpreted as 1-gauging the discrete two-form symmetry along the wall. Hanany-Witten brane crossing determines its action on charged defects.

Reduce a candidate R7 worldvolume topological subsector, imported from earlier work, in differential cohomology. For the Ω-brane its terms are ∫(H3⋆f6 + F5⋆f4 + H7⋆f2), with bulk differential characters coupled to worldvolume fields that absorb ending brane charges.

Current-conservation constraints become differential operators on conformal tensor structures. Integrated Ward identities, charge-conservation identities involving the stress tensor, and weakly broken Ward identities combine with Anselmi’s trick to constrain leading behavior near the HS point.

Regularized first-order conformal perturbation theory extracts dimension shifts from the logarithmic divergence of integrated ⟨JℓJℓO⟩. The resulting evolution equation is dΔℓ/dt=−C_JJO, where C_JJO is a particular weighted linear combination of spinning OPE coefficients.

For moduli couplings, the authors expand the supergravity action and matter Kähler metrics around stabilized values, diagonalize kinetic/mass terms, canonically normalize matter, and extract cubic interactions after electroweak symmetry breaking and use of fermion equations of motion. Heavy stabilized directions are integrated out for the fibre potential.

A conformal transformation uses F=∂f/∂R>0, g̃μν=F gμν and φ/MP=√(3/2) ln F. The Einstein-frame potential is U/F². Matter coupling is obtained both from the stress-tensor trace in the scalar equation and from the cubic fermion interaction.

The higher-curvature route is assessed through schematic dimensional reduction of ten-dimensional α′ corrections and comparison of the four-dimensional suppression scales of R² and R⁴ terms. The reviewed analysis distinguishes heterotic/type-I nonzero leading R² coefficients from their absence in type IIB.

A numerical algorithm builds the descent path by minimizing the potential in a neighborhood of each successive point. The full-model run uses 24 points; distance increments are evaluated with the field-space metric, and εV and the minimum covariant-Hessian eigenvalue are evaluated along the path.

Analytic exponential-potential lemmas are combined with numerical reductions: dilaton plus overall volume, those fields plus two B-field axions, and all seven saxions with axions fixed to zero. Quadratic B-field terms are retained in the numerical axion model to avoid distorting its runaway behavior.

The author selects compact-group-manifold solutions with a single tachyon, uses MSSV consistent-truncation data for the potential and field metric, and studies the potential along the canonically normalized tachyonic eigenvector before constructing the descent trajectory.

Explicit cutoff functions are obtained from genus-one topological free energy. The holomorphic anomaly equation and boundary asymptotics determine F1 up to an additive constant; numerical distance calculations and asymptotic expansions yield field-range formulas.

The argument combines species counting, de Sitter entropy or a smallest-black-hole horizon comparison, and the emergent-string constraint on asymptotic species-scale decay. It then determines allowed field ranges by imposing the potential threshold against the cutoff.

The range is defined using the longest minimal geodesics satisfying V0≤Λs² and decomposed into left tail, fixed bulk segment and right tail. If only one infinite-distance limit is present, one endpoint is instead fixed at the desert point and the other tail has zero length.

Shell motion is rewritten as a one-dimensional potential problem with an initial-value constraint. Axial exterior perturbations use Reissner–Nordström master potentials and tortoise coordinates; the interior gravitational potential is l(l+1)/R².

Newtonian energy bookkeeping includes rest energy, electric and gravitational contributions, and adiabatic internal energy satisfying dU=−P dA. This motivates examining negative surface pressure before the relativistic treatment.

Israel matching gives the conserved gravitational energy m=M√(1+Ṙ²)−(M²−Q²)/(2R). Static configurations are tested by stationarity and positive second derivative of the rest-configuration energy. General parameter regions are solved numerically after normalizing charge and radius by m0.

For an illustrative particle-creation argument, the author assumes a spatially flat background with a(η)=C+D tanh(Eη), C=(aBi+aBf)/2 and D=(aBf−aBi)/2. It approaches constant scale factors as η→±∞; particle production is invoked from cited curved-spacetime QFT results rather than calculated explicitly.

The imported suppression mechanism combines Gibbs–Duhem dp/dT=S/V with the Bekenstein bound S≤2πRE. Saturating that bound and setting R to the horizon distance gives dp/dT=2πRHorρ, followed by an integrated pressure ratio pT/pF=exp(−2πI).

Integration of the fluid conservation equation supplies the Chaplygin density interpolation. The scenario identifies the early matter-like regime as the B-phase and the later approximately constant-density regime as the A-phase.

Extract kinetic coefficients from genus-one two-point amplitudes by relaxing momentum conservation while retaining each external state's mass-shell condition. Expand in p1·p2 and match the coefficient to the effective action, including the Einstein–Hilbert contribution.

Use image-charge Green functions, theta-function spin sums and Ramond index traces. Analyze local vertex-collision integrals first at positive δ=α′p1·p2, then continue to small δ; these integrals can lower the apparent momentum order.

Form overlap and Laplacian matrices OAB=〈αA,αB〉 and ΔAB=〈αA,ΔαB〉, evaluate integrals by Monte Carlo, and solve Δv=λOv. Rescaling the O-orthogonal eigenvectors gives orthonormal modes and a trivial matter metric in that basis.

For hypersurfaces, approximate the Calabi–Yau metric by an algebraic Kähler potential K=(πkh)−1 log(sαhαβ̄s̄β), optimized using an energy functional. The associated fibre metric G=(sαhαβ̄s̄β)−m/kh is asserted to satisfy HYM for the chosen Kähler metric.

Construct finite sets of charge-correct homogeneous monomials and differential forms, indexed by degree kφ, for positive and negative m. Remove linear dependencies; on hypersurfaces, pull back the ambient basis and remove relations induced by Q=0.

The AdS/CFT dictionary maps orbital angular momentum to boundary spin and orbital energy to a Regge trajectory. Small radial oscillations are normalized to boundary time; Bohr–Sommerfeld-type quantization supplies radial excitation corrections suppressed relative to the heavy-probe limit.

The point-particle action reduces motion to an effective radial potential V. Circular orbits satisfy V=V′=0, while marginal stability adds V″=0. Energy and angular momentum are expanded at large radius, then the radius is eliminated to express energy in conserved quantities.
Large-L perturbation theory gives analytic small-black-hole ISCO expressions. Large extremal black holes are treated analytically for neutral probes and investigated numerically for charged probes.

Canonical normalization is treated through factorizations of nonminimal kinetic matrices that preserve determinant phases. Numerical diagonalization and fits test whether modular textures can accommodate quark and lepton data.

Heavy fields are integrated out using a Schur complement and holomorphic gauge-kinetic thresholds. Supergravity analysis tracks Kähler transformations, chiral anomalies, and gluino phases; the appendix includes one-loop gluino contributions required for consistent modular transformation properties.

Holomorphic modular-form weight counting constrains Yukawas and their determinants. E4 and E6 generate the forms; weight zero permits only a constant. CP violation is diagnosed with Jarlskog-type invariants, which are nonholomorphic and therefore need not share the determinant restriction.

Separate intra-meson from inter-meson diagrams. Large-N factorization makes the latter suppressed by 1/N; without operator mixing, intra-meson contributions cancel in γ(double meson)−2γ(single meson). With mixing, compare the relevant eigenvalues instead.

Compute ultraviolet-divergent parts of one-loop composite-operator correlation functions, subtract external-field renormalization, and extract anomalous dimensions. Chiral spinor projections and Fierz identities place fermionic amplitudes into a common operator basis; scalar/tensor double-meson mixing requires diagonalizing a renormalization matrix.

Use the classification of extremal elliptic K3 fibrations and Shioda–Tate to identify maximal non-Abelian points. For proposed rank-17 studies, examine embeddings H⊕G into the Néron–Severi lattice, requiring the embedded hyperbolic plane to contain a pseudo-ample class.

Use D2,3≅H2 and the correspondence between O+(L2,3) modular forms and even-weight genus-two Siegel modular forms. The reviewed parameter identification is α=−ψ4/48, β=−ψ6/864, γ=−4χ10, δ=χ12, with the stated scale qualifications.

Analyze y²=x³+(αt4+γt3)x+t7+βt6+δt5 through Δ=t9[4(αt+γ)³+27t(t²+βt+δ)²]. Degeneration types locate gauge enhancements; the reviewed 5-brane loci are γ=0 and q=0, with q an explicit polynomial in the coefficients.

For Λ ≫ mV, evaluate Bnon-grav approximately as (4/π) times the integral from Λ² to infinity of Im Mnon-grav(s,0)/(s − 2mV²)³. Extract Bgrav from the finite t-channel Taylor coefficient after pole and kinematic subtraction.
Use forward dispersion relations after subtracting the graviton t-channel pole. For spin 1, first remove kinematic singularities; organize the result as B = Bnon-grav + Bgrav.

Compute one-loop diagrams with FeynRules, FeynArts, FeynCalc and Package-X. For other gravitational diagrams, introduce a graviton-propagator IR regulator; the appendix estimates their contribution as O(1/(MPl²Λ²)), subdominant in the regime studied.

Treat the sector label as part of the bundle of partition functions over moduli space, pass to the subgroup that fixes that label, and normalize the corresponding moduli integral by the cover's volume.

Average over the theory-label parameters m, keep x external, and change variables by a group element. Measure preservation and joint covariance then remove the transformed external argument from the integral.

Choose a modular-compatible sector sum associated with a gaugeable Lagrangian subgroup, or pair opposite quadratic forms and contract corresponding discriminant labels. Check both finite representation invariance and scalar automorphy factors.

Specify the subgroup and weight, verify square integrability, and project the function onto its discrete and continuous spectral modes. In the Narain application, moduli dependence resides in the coefficients of a τ-dependent basis.

The perturbative argument uses the resummed one-loop graviton propagator in flat d-dimensional spacetime, a spin-weighted massless count N₀, the Lambert W₋₁ branch, and large-N₀/Stirling expansions. Massive KK contributions are treated through a heat-kernel trace.

For higher-derivative corrections, the discussion uses Wald entropy, attractor equations, and prepotential homogeneity to express entropy as a Legendre transform of mixed black-hole free energy. Entropy minimization then connects S_sp to topological free energy; this argument is explicitly credited to prior work.

The proposed minimal-black-hole algorithm minimizes charges while requiring entropy to grow at weak coupling or large volume. The growth requirement is intended to retain a trustworthy effective description while shrinking the horizon.

Contrast the QFT species prescription Λ̃∼Mpl/√Nsp with Nsp counting states below Λ̃, against the black-hole prescription identifying Nsp with the entropy of the smallest EFT black hole. The actual emergence computations use the QFT prescription.

Use field-theory one-loop wave-function corrections, summed over states below the cutoff. Moduli contributions depend on derivatives of tower masses; near the string-like cutoff they scale as sums of degeneracy times ∂aM∂bM. Gauge corrections use sums of degeneracy times electric-charge products.

Approximate dense excitation sums by multidimensional integrals, transform the mass constraint into a spherical domain, and use the asymptotic oscillator degeneracy. Species-scale equations are treated through Lambert-W asymptotics; angular integrals determine vanishing cross terms and relative metric coefficients.

Split Φ into its expectation value and fluctuations, integrate out reservoir degrees of freedom, and express temporal memory terms through a derivative expansion. For sufficiently slow evolution, its leading dissipative contribution is Υφ̇; perturbative and resummation details are deferred.

Estimate thermal fluctuation freeze-out by comparing mode damping with expansion, obtaining k_F² ≈ (3H + Υ)H. Model examples use distributed shifted masses or a two-stage interaction in which inflaton-coupled heavy fields communicate with light decay products.

String-derived mode-dependent couplings soften sums over exchanged KK states. Their Fourier transform describes a localized current with Gaussian width σ = √(ln Δ) l_s, where Δ > 1 depends on the compactification.

Compute the one-loop Wilson-line potential using a Schwinger proper-time representation and Poisson resummation of the complete KK tower. The calculation separates the zero dual-lattice contribution from the field-dependent terms.

Use normalized Fourier expansions for periodic circle fields and cosine/sine expansions on S¹/Z₂. Even interval fields obey Neumann conditions and retain zero modes; odd fields obey Dirichlet conditions and have no zero modes.

Tadpole diagrams are organized in a small background-displacement expansion. Newton iteration Φ(n+1)=Φ(n)−V′/V″ is adapted from prior work to interpret resummations and identify candidate endpoint extrema.

Imported Riemann/Kähler normal-coordinate techniques locally normalize scalar kinetic terms. Four-point scalar amplitudes combine curvature-induced derivative interactions with potential contact and exchange contributions.

The central argument substitutes black-hole charge and mass into an inverse-square force comparison: Fe=Q²/r² and Fg=M²/r². The adopted condition Q/M>1 is then used to infer electromagnetic dominance.

The authors present radial metric-function plots for selected parameters and interpret their zeros as evidence of horizons with Q/M>1. This illustrates their proposed compatibility between the adopted WGC condition and weak cosmic censorship.

Threshold decomposition starts with Feynman prescriptions for every propagator, integrates loop energies by residues, cancels pseudothresholds and separates principal-value terms from threshold delta functions. The fakeon prescription then deletes delta terms containing any fakeon frequency, before the remaining spatial integrations, and excludes fakeons from external states.

Renormalization is organized using BRST and Batalin–Vilkovisky master equations. Divergences are separated into gauge-invariant local terms and a σ-exact contribution; canonical field/source transformations remove the latter, leaving counterterms with the original action's operator content. The cohomological theorem underlying this separation is imported rather than proved here.

Inflationary calculations use auxiliary fields and field redefinitions to expose the wrong-sign mode, eliminate it using the classical fakeon Green function, and reduce the projected action to Mukhanov–Sasaki form. Mode functions obey Bunch–Davies conditions; slow-roll and renormalization-group techniques organize the spectra.

An illustrative compactification of the M2 effective action introduces R = gsls and ls² = l³/R. Kaluza–Klein reduction along a brane direction gives the tension and Newton-constant scaling identified with type IIA fundamental strings. This step uses established string-theory identifications and introduces a scale through R.

Canonical dimensional analysis, using [ϕ] = (p−1)/2, is combined with the dual-brane relation p̃ = D−p−4. Subtracting the original and dual dimensional equations yields (D−2p−4)(4−2n) = 0, separating the equal-dimensional-brane branch from the exceptional n = 2 branch.

Allowability is tested by seeking a complex radial curve γ from 0 to v satisfying |arg γ′²|+3|arg a(γ)²|<π everywhere. An extremal curve saturates this inequality and starts at angle π/8; its position relative to v bounds whether an allowable contour can reach the endpoint.

In the solvable model, a coordinate transformation and hyperbolic field variables turn the Euclidean action quadratic. Explicit saddle solutions and the integrated extremal-curve relation yield an asymptotic critical boundary in minisuperspace, which is compared with classical histories obtained from the imaginary saddle action.

For slow-roll models, the authors numerically solve the complex boundary-value problem and integrate the extremal curve together with the background fields. They scan potential parameters and use increasing numerical precision to check convergence. The supplement describes accompanying Mathematica code and data, which are not independently evaluated in this pass.

Background equations are expanded to first order in the small running parameter. Synchronous-gauge linear perturbations are treated iteratively and implemented with the background equations in a modified CLASS Einstein–Boltzmann solver.

MontePython Metropolis–Hastings sampling uses Planck 2018 variants, Pantheon+, BAO and cosmic chronometers, with and without SH0ES calibration. Chains stop at Gelman–Rubin R−1<0.005. Model comparison uses ΔDIC=DICΛCDM−DICStRVM, positive values favoring StRVM.

For EH, approximate the proper-time integral using separate small-s and large-s expansions, numerically solve the degeneracy condition, and integrate the mass formula. DBI admits an analytic degeneracy radius in flat space and a mass expression involving a Gauss hypergeometric function.

Express the mass as M(rH,n), impose horizon degeneracy through ∂M/∂rH=0, and evaluate the mass at the resulting radius. Magnetic flux is fixed by charge quantization; electric solutions use a Legendre transform to a conjugate tensor Pμν with a standard divergence-free equation.

For disjoint fields with K = K^(1) + K^(2) and W = W^(1) + W^(2), apply GFL independently to each completely decoupled sector. Compare this with mediation that leaves visible and hidden sectors interacting in the formal global limit.

Insert the quoted electron mass, approximately 0.5 × 10^-3 GeV, and squared electromagnetic coupling, approximately 0.1, into GFL; then identify the interacting theory's vacuum energy with the supersymmetry-breaking contribution.

Use curvature-dominated small-ξ initial conditions and shoot in the bubble-size parameter η; determine the brane position from junction consistency, switch on the exterior flux potential, and match the Minkowski asymptotics. Dimensionless solutions give Stot=(Mp⁴/U0)S̄.

Reduce to an Einstein-frame volume modulus and a Coleman-De Luccia ansatz ds₄²=dξ²+ρ(ξ)²dΩ₃². Derive bulk equations and brane jump conditions, retaining the gravitational subtraction and boundary terms associated with the apparent reduced-space singularity.

For the Dirac spectrum, conformally separate the S³ factor, expand in sphere eigenspinors, and solve coupled radial equations by shooting on a finite interval. Wall regularity and self-adjoint boundary conditions define the numerical problem.
Displace the free vacuum by Df=exp(−i∫fπ), giving the Hertzberg kink state Df|H〉. Conjugate H to H′=Df†HDf and expand by field order; the classical equation eliminates the linear term.

For time-dependent f, use Df(t)=exp[i∫(ḟϕ−fπ)] and a comoving frame. Its time-translation generator is H̃′=Df†HDf−iDf†∂tDf; including the derivative term cancels the tadpole by the classical equation.

Expand fluctuations in Sturm–Liouville normal modes: a translational zero mode, continuum modes and possible discrete shape modes. A Bogoliubov transformation relates these operators to plane-wave operators and diagonalizes the leading quadratic kink Hamiltonian.
Stack a G-symmetric TQFT on a submanifold before gauging the diagonal symmetry. The TQFT becomes a theta defect in the gauged theory, with fusion inherited from stacking the TQFTs.

Finite abelian gauging is formulated as a sum over flat background configurations with a Pontryagin-dual pairing. An alternative two-dimensional construction uses a triangulation-dual mesh, algebra objects and their bimodules.

The SymTFT sandwich places a (d+1)-dimensional topological theory between a symmetry boundary and a physical boundary. Interval compactification recovers the QFT; bulk defects organize symmetry defects and generalized charges.

Reviews one-loop modulus wavefunction renormalization from mass-dependent scalar and fermion couplings, summing states below the species cutoff and replacing sums by integrals at large species number.

Computes curved-background functional determinants using an adiabatic expansion, Wick rotation and a species momentum cutoff. Scalar and fermion curvature shifts are respectively 2H² and 3H²; these do not affect the leading heavy-tower potential.

The anholonomic frame and connection deformation method uses a canonical shell-adapted connection, related to Levi-Civita by distortion, to decouple modified Ricci equations and integrate them through generating functions, effective sources, and integration data.

Generalize Perelman F/W functionals by prescribed star products and integration ordering; formulate Hamilton-type equations symbolically and sketch a shell-adapted variational construction for selected κ-linear configurations.

The isocurvature mode is isolated by taking Φ→0, equivalent at leading order in V_a/V_i to setting C_1=0. Power spectra and their k derivatives give amplitudes, cross-correlation and spectral indices.

A separate-universe argument relates patch-dependent inflation duration to axion rolling. The δN calculation evaluates curvature between an initially flat hypersurface and a final uniform-density hypersurface; inflation ends at constant φ_i.

Linearized Einstein and Klein–Gordon equations are solved in the superhorizon slow-roll limit. Non-decreasing modes C_1 and C_3 are matched to independent Gaussian field fluctuations at horizon crossing using the Bunch–Davies prescription.

Perturbative dilatation-operator diagonalization in scalar and derivative subsectors; contour projection of free partition functions and the superconformal index tests the constrained-magnon counting.

Conformal-ladder resummation, contour deformation and Bessel representations organize correlators; heavy-light conformal blocks extract OPE data. Supersymmetric localization supplies emergent matrix integrals for integrated observables.

Short-representation theory and closure of the centrally extended algebra constrain energies and interactions. Semiclassical expansion about a sourced large-charge saddle supplies additional information.

Solve Picard–Fuchs equations in Frobenius bases and determine transition matrices to integral monodromy weight frames. Hypergeometric examples permit analytic computations; other examples use numerical computations followed by arithmetic matching.

Use nilpotent orbits, monodromy weight filtrations, Deligne splittings and extension data to construct limiting mixed Hodge structures (LMHS) in integral frames. Instanton maps constrained by Griffiths transversality generate the near-boundary period expansions.
Estimate one-loop wavefunction corrections by summing heavy towers up to Λ, using Λ≃N_Fi m_Fi. The weighted sums of n² logarithms yield kinetic coefficients scaling as f_F† diag[(Λ/m_Fi)³] f_F.

Factor kinetic matrices as k=X†X and use invertible field redefinitions to move flavor information between noncanonical kinetic coefficients and ordinary Yukawa matrices. Arbitrary complex matrices W parameterize the nonuniqueness of this representation.
Use the imported instanton corrected HK construction and HK/QK correspondence, then express the QK twistor contact structure explicitly through the HK data and Bessel-function series.

Directly Poisson resum the contact form to obtain type IIB Darboux coordinates. Via the quantum corrected mirror map, lift S-duality to twistor space and establish holomorphicity, contact-distribution preservation and compatibility with the real structure.
Introduce a radial metric deformation e^(2σ1)dz². Its Einstein–Hilbert contribution supplies a term linear in ∂zσ1, allowing cancellation of the term linear in ∂zα generated by squaring the flux.

For flux variations use a gauge potential in the Poincaré patch: Cp = e^α Ĉp, p = d−1. The resulting external field strength is Fd = (−1)^p e^α(p−z∂zα)vold; magnetic flux is obtained by Hodge-dualizing this external flux.

Promote constant solution parameters to spacetime-dependent fields, extract their two-derivative coefficients, then use the resulting metric along constant, on-shell variations. Weyl transformations, dimensional reduction and integration by parts retain derivatives of the volume factor.

The reviewed arrival-direction analysis uses an unbinned likelihood with directional exposure, a weighted von Mises–Fisher source distribution, and an isotropic background. Its likelihood-ratio statistic tests isotropy; scanning the energy threshold incurs a Monte Carlo estimated trial penalty. This supplies context for the source selection.

The authors maximize an energy likelihood, expressed as a product of normalized spectra above a threshold, fitting γ and Ec separately in 20° windows around NGC 4945, NGC 253, M83, NGC 1068, and NGC 891. They report marginalized 68% parameter intervals and display 68% and 95% contour regions.

Define the metric-measure Laplacian through the subdifferential of relaxed Cheeger energy. The proof relates Δu=0 to Ch(u)=0, then establishes constancy using Poincaré inequalities or the smooth geometry outside a negligible singular set.

Use Rayleigh quotients and generalized Cheeger constants h0,h1, defined by weighted boundary/bulk ratios of finite-volume disjoint sets. Bounds imported from the authors' earlier work connect these constants to low spin-two masses; h0→0 with h1 finite targets an isolated light mode.

Complementary computations use Narain/Mikhailov lattice embeddings and parent heterotic models, fractional null junctions and Mordell–Weil sections. Orbifold symmetry computations compare boundary fundamental-group abelianization with BPS-quiver methods.
Relative homology/cohomology sequences, intersection matrices, Smith normal form and boundary linking pairings translate wrapped-brane charges and screening into defect-group data.
Reduce the 11d Chern–Simons coupling with torsional boundary flux represented by fractional Cartan-flux shifts Fa → Fa + λa B/N; extract fractional instanton couplings and mixed anomalies.

Use integral inequalities and an integrable nonnegative Lipschitz distance for global convergence; use Gram matrices, field rotations, and convex geometry to characterize scaling powers and acceleration bounds.
Rewrite the exact scalar-field and Friedmann equations as autonomous ODEs using Hubble-normalized velocities and potential amplitudes, then reparameterize time and analyze critical points.

Organize expected corrections by physical origin, solve for shifted vevs to leading order in their coefficients, and evaluate the corrected vacuum energy. Analyze non-perturbative no-scale behavior using V=νgs exp(t/gs), τs=t/a and corrections with exponential weight λ.

Construct the four-dimensional supergravity scalar potential from warped Kähler and flux/nonperturbative superpotentials, adding the exact anti-brane uplift proportional to h^−1/V². Expand conifold stabilization perturbatively in 1/β and exhibit critical points of the full leading potential.

Reduce first on S²×S² to six dimensions, then project the remaining angular dependence onto asymptotic KK zero modes to extract five-dimensional metric and scalar profiles. Use analytic single-stack examples and numerical breathing/squashing profiles to characterize the ETW region.

Use the known harmonic-function construction on a hyperelliptic surface, branch-point degenerations, flux quantization and asymptotic expansions to identify pipes, five-brane regions and smooth caps. Five-brane neighborhoods are checked for finite transverse distance rather than assumed to generate additional asymptotic throats.

Use Calabi–Vesentini coordinates and the compact Maurer–Cartan connection to calculate the composite U(1) potential, then change to tube-domain coordinates to identify the compensating phase with an orthogonal automorphy factor.

Control zeros and poles through the input's principal part and Heegner divisors. Existence of a prescribed principal part is tested by its vanishing pairing with all cusp forms of weight 1+l/2 for the dual Weil representation.

Apply imported theta-lift/Borcherds-product results: an input of weight 1−l/2 produces an orthogonal modular form of weight c(0,0)/2. The stated theorem assumes l≥3, integral negative Fourier coefficients, a primitive isotropic vector, and an additional isotropic vector in K.

Review prior two-axion calculations of scalar spectra, PBH abundances and induced gravitational waves, and prior late-time fits using a one-loop logarithmic curvature action. The detailed numerical and likelihood analyses are assigned to the cited works.

Estimate the gravitational anomaly condensate from chiral graviton modes with a UV cutoff, combine the anomaly-current and axion equations, and derive RVM evolution through conservation of total stress energy. The Cotton contribution itself is not separately conserved.

Implement the modified three-form Bianchi identity as a path-integral delta constraint using a canonically normalized multiplier b. Integration over the nondynamical three-form yields its kinetic term and coupling to RṘ−F F̃, within the stated derivative truncation and boundary assumptions.

Use a rudimentary N-body calculation with classical gravitational accelerations and leapfrog position/velocity updates. Black holes start on a regular lattice with random masses and velocities, while periodic boundary images approximate a three-torus.

Assess larger-scale binding using spherical Newtonian-shell collapse. After a static free-fall comparison, numerically evolve the time-dependent horizon radius and density using RK4 to obtain the shell-collapse time; the static estimate has an explicit factor-of-two mass caveat.

Represent mergers as perfectly inelastic collisions: masses add, velocity follows linear-momentum conservation, and position is the unweighted midpoint. A pair merges when separation is at most min(10mi,10mj); corresponding boundary images are updated together.

Reviews the imported N=2 black-hole motivation using D0/D4 charges, attractor equations, genus-one higher-derivative corrections and Wald entropy. Special charges with vanishing cubic intersection contribution but nonzero c2i pi yield Smin≈F1 within the supergravity regime.

Computes topological free energy through an infinite mass determinant and lattice factors m+nT. Strictly massless contributions are omitted to remove an infrared divergence; ultraviolet sums use Riemann zeta regularization. The topological spectrum excludes oscillator modes also present after decompactification.

Rewrites the background equations as a six-variable autonomous system, eliminating Ωm with the Friedmann constraint. Late-time analysis combines fixed-λ,Qm snapshots in (x,y) with a four-variable system that retains evolving λ and Qm.

Uses transformations through z,ξ and then u,v to expose critical points, followed by Jacobian eigenvalues and numerical evolution for zero-eigenvalue families. Appendix A instead uses ϕ as a clock and linearizes the slow-roll system in scalar velocity, entropy density, and matter density.

Reviews special chiral-superfield constructions, eliminates auxiliary and three-form fields, and retains the boundary terms required for a well-posed variational problem. Gravitational actions also require the Gibbons–Hawking term.

Uses false-vacuum action subtraction for noncompact gravitational solutions, matching the cutoff in the physical scale factor ρ. Authors compare rigid action extrema with zero nucleation energy, and the illustrated nearly Minkowski gravitational bounce with vanishing ADM mass.

Solves O(4)-symmetric Euclidean equations with overshoot/undershoot shooting. The scalar is continuous across the membrane, while its first derivative jumps; gravity adds a jump in the metric derivative. Fixed-radius solutions are evaluated as a family to locate an extremum of the action.

Reviews the Ostrogradsky Hamiltonian construction and compares canonical and alternative oscillator Fock representations, their wavefunction normalizability, norms, velocity-squared expectations, propagator pole prescriptions, and Wick rotation behavior.

Reviews Schwinger–Keldysh expectation-value equations for local fields. The reported Maxwell example replaces in-out kernels by real, causal in-in kernels and includes gravitational source/observer correlations to obtain a gauge-independent effective equation.

For de Sitter secular effects, reviews integrating out differentiated B fields at constant A to obtain a curvature-induced logarithmic effective potential, followed by a stochastic Langevin treatment. A broader proposed resummation combines stochastic methods with curvature-dependent renormalization-group effects.

Constructs global distributional modes as boundary values from complex de Sitter tubes. Integrals over an orbital basis of the future null cone yield analytic two-point kernels; the local Hadamard condition fixes normalization, and Wightman reconstruction supplies the field operator.

Uses ambient-space Casimir equations and intertwining identities to express the tensor through vector and scalar ingredients. The physical vector ingredient is built from a conformally coupled scalar plane wave (x·ξ/R)^(−2), with ξ null.

Quantize the symmetry TFT using a Heisenberg extension of H^k(M,D). Flux operators act as clock and shift operators on a polarization-dependent basis; absolute partition functions are overlaps between the relative partition vector and topological boundary states.

For cyclic polarization pairs denoted here by (u,v), gauging is a discrete Fourier transform implementing (u,v)→((−1)^(k−1)v,u). Allowed counterterms change v→v+ru. Gauging twice returns the original theory in 4s+2 dimensions and its charge-conjugated version in 4s dimensions.

Thermal partition-function derivatives determine energy, specific heat and pressure fluctuations. Linearized Einstein constraints then relate density fluctuations to scalar metric perturbations and off-diagonal stresses to gravitational waves.

Double Field Theory (DFT) doubles spatial coordinates and combines the metric and antisymmetric tensor into a generalized metric. Symmetry arguments organize all-order α′ corrections in a homogeneous, isotropic minisuperspace action.

Matrix constructions use a high-temperature Matsubara expansion, temporal-matrix eigenvalues and spatial submatrices to define emergent geometry. Numerical results and the Gaussian expansion method inform symmetry-breaking arguments.

Rewrite parent theories in N=(0,1) multiplets, impose orientifold invariance of the quiver and superpotential, and determine Chan–Paton projections and Fermi transformations. Connect the field involution to geometry through mesonic generators, Hilbert series and the Poincaré-residue description of the holomorphic four-form.

Reduce IIB topological terms on ∂X to a 5D symmetry TFT, and encode defect actions through 7-brane monodromies and branch cuts. In the supplied su(2) triality example, string-junction lines are analyzed through the total monodromy; trivial coker(ρ−1) implies no additional lines coupling to B2,C2.

For the flat deformations, compute the KK spectrum by replacing circle momentum with a charge-dependent shifted momentum, multiplied by e⁻ψ. Supersymmetry enhancement is detected through gravitini attaining conformal dimension Δ=3/2.

Add a form potential by twisting the frame with exp(C). Within this construction, consistency holds iff ρ⁻¹F in flat indices is constant. Flux invariant under the subgroup containing U gives a simple sufficient implementation.

Generalized Scherk–Schwarz reduction factors internal dependence into an E8(8) twist U and density ρ. Generalized-frame closure with constant X, L_UM UN=XMNP UP, supplies the embedding tensor and consistency criterion.

Studies turning points of the Euclidean Friedmann constraint and evaluates the on-shell action by quadrature between minimum and maximum scale factors. The d=3 metric and action are explicit; the d=4 action is integrated numerically and compared with a linear flux approximation.

For four-dimensional scalar perturbations, expands in spherical harmonics, imposes Hamiltonian constraints, constructs a gauge-invariant flux fluctuation and conjugate momentum, and obtains a quadratic action. Periodic boundary conditions remove the boundary contribution; positivity of its coefficients is examined numerically.

Wick-rotates across slices of vanishing extrinsic curvature and uses an effective scale-factor potential to distinguish Lorentzian branches. Continues the fluctuation equations to examine the arrow of time, using a weak-charge expansion and numerical higher-charge comparisons.

Reduce RR potentials on harmonic and light exact/coexact forms, then match wrapped-brane DBI masses and tensions to BPS EFT charges. In the one-mode example this identifies the normalized reduction forms with smeared calibrated-cycle currents.

Expand the distributional current δ(Πp) in orthonormal eigenforms satisfying Δbi=λi²bi, with coefficients obtained by integrating their Hodge duals over Πp. Define δsm by retaining modes with λi≪ℓs mKK.

Express the torsion linking pairing as L=Σi ci ei/λi mod 1. Its smeared version Lsm restricts the same sum to retained light modes; this follows using the compatibility of d and the Hodge star with the Laplacian.

Expand the Einstein-Hilbert action retaining compact-coordinate derivatives of gij; vary the reduced fields and separate gij(xi,x3) = χ(x3) gij^(3)(xi). Solve the nonlinear profile equation perturbatively and impose circle periodicity.

Transform to the three-dimensional Einstein frame and combine the tree-level radion potential with one-loop Casimir energies expressed through K2 Bessel functions. Use the expanded potential, its extrema and vacuum energy sign to obtain parameter constraints.

Integrate fermions and ghosts algebraically to obtain determinants. Fermionic kinetic and mass matrices scale respectively as λ³ and λ⁴ under L → λL, allowing polynomial bounds on the remaining edge integral.

Introduce spherical edge coordinates |Lε| = r fε(θ), exploit homogeneous scaling of discretized actions, and split integration into small-r and large-r regions. Compare radial powers against convergence bounds.

Define bosonic matter integrals using Euclidean lengths L̃ε = |Lε| and Euclidean actions, then define their Lorentzian counterparts through the stated Wick map. Gauge-fix Yang-Mills theory and include Faddeev-Popov ghosts.
Extremize and minimize generalized entropy over both island I and radiation region R. Use bulk RT surfaces of connected and disconnected topology; DGP terms add brane-boundary area contributions.

Motivate the modified island prescription using replica path integrals, induced higher-curvature gravity and replica-entropy RG invariance. The metric saddle yields the background geometry, while defining R dynamically supplies the additional extremization over R.

Analyze the intermediate description through perturbative Hilbert-space mode counting and scalar KK decomposition. Mixed Dirichlet/Neumann boundary conditions and paired Green functions are used to examine low-energy causal correlators.

Extremize bulk area plus brane-intersection contributions: S=min ext[A/(4G_{d+1})+sum_i A_tilde_i/(4G_{b,i})]. Variation gives a bulk Euler–Lagrange ODE and coupling-dependent dynamical endpoint conditions.

Numerically shoot static extremal surfaces from either brane, infer the other coupling through endpoint conditions, and compare numerical surface entropy with analytic horizon entropy. Large, potentially unstable-area solutions are discarded.

Temporarily relax flux quantization to shift axions to zero and nonrolling saxions to one; then expand stationarity equations at large saxion values and examine potential values and Hessian stability. The rescalings preserve W and rescale V by a positive overall factor.

Search for asymptotic slow-roll gradient flows by parametrizing saxions as powers of a common parameter and taking ratios of their equations of motion. Competing monomials determine possible exponents and coefficient ratios.

For the conjectural tower mechanism, reduce a real five-dimensional scalar with two exponential interactions on a circle. Retaining its zero mode and first KK mode produces modified Bessel I0 interactions and permits illustrative nonzero KK-field extrema.

Uses Bayesian posterior inference and evidence ratios for model comparison, implemented through ENTERPRISE and the new PTArcade wrapper. Reports marginalized credible regions rather than independently validated parameter determinations.

SIGW spectra use a convolution quadratic in the primordial scalar spectrum, with delta, Gaussian-in-log-k and box templates. Production assumes radiation domination and Gaussian scalar statistics. Associated PBH bounds use Press–Schechter spherical collapse.
Models residuals as δt=n+Fa+Mϵ. Analytically marginalizes Fourier coefficients and linear timing offsets, using flat priors for the latter; deterministic signals enter through δt→δt−h(θ).

Compute scalar charge-to-mass vectors and project them onto asymptotic geodesic tangents. Use local convex-hull plots and direction-dependent max-α plots to distinguish local scalar bounds from the decay rate of the leading light tower.

Match gravitational and gauge actions and identify dual BPS states to express heterotic masses in Type I′ variables B,C. Determine the moduli metric by fixing BPS scalar charge-to-mass vectors, with a separate dimensional-reduction treatment, then introduce flat coordinates.

Dimensionally reduce the warped ten-dimensional background, perform the Einstein-frame Weyl rescaling, and obtain high-excitation KK mass scaling from self-adjoint mode equations using WKB. The explicit calculations treat dilaton and RR one-form modes before arguing universality for massless ten-dimensional fields.
Compare extensive EFT entropy S_EFT∼N0 ΛUV^(d−1) vol with the holographic area bound. For N0 of order one, this gives ΛUV^(d−1)≲A/vol in Planck units.

For multiplicative towers, combine densities as p_eff=Σp_t and masses by a density-weighted geometric average. Translate tower vectors z_t into effective species vectors Z_eff=(Σp_t z_t)/(d−2+Σp_t), then construct their convex hull.

Solve the Einstein–scalar domain-wall equations to identify geodesic trajectories. With exponential potentials, introduce constrained dimensionless flow variables x,y and classify asymptotic attractors and repellers.

Constructs neutrino KK mass matrices, obtains spectra through transcendental eigenvalue equations, and uses normalized eigenvectors for mixing weights. The appendix sums vacuum oscillation amplitudes over KK modes and compares illustrative survival probabilities with the SM case.

Uses a classical runaway potential plus one-loop Casimir contributions expressed through modified Bessel functions, a step-function approximation to particle thresholds, and parameter scans classifying radion extrema as dS, AdS, or absent.
