Import a sufficient nonacceleration theorem for sums of scalar exponentials: with positive coefficients, one common field direction whose minimum exponent is at least 2/√(d−2) suffices. The stated extension with negative coefficients requires additional componentwise exponent ordering.

Apply dimensional reduction recursively to higher-dimensional exponential rolling potentials. The argument uses the absence of acceleration, or of a potential altogether, in the listed fundamental 10D/11D theories to exclude this proposed loophole.
Compare radius scaling of potential sources, reduce the Einstein-Hilbert action, perform a Weyl rescaling to d-dimensional Einstein frame, and canonically normalize the logarithmic volume modulus.

Represent selected constant-angle trajectories using individually constant velocity ratios; investigate departures from the boundary through an inverse-power expansion of the single-plane deviation angle θ(s).

Project covariant scalar equations onto tangent and turning-normal directions, combine with Friedmann equations, and compute turning directly from the field-space connection. The projected equations include Φ̈+3HΦ̇+V_T=0 and ΩΦ̇=V_N.

The production estimate expands bulk fields into Fourier KK modes and sums graviton-to-radion-plus-lighter-graviton decay channels. The abundance estimate then uses a homogeneous scalar equation, a quadratic potential near its minimum, and radiation/matter redshifting.

Dimensional reduction of the five-dimensional Einstein–cosmological-constant action to the four-dimensional Einstein frame is used to identify the radion kinetic term and exponential potential. The authors relate compact-radius growth by N e-folds to noncompact Einstein-frame growth by 3N/2 e-folds.

The primordial tensor spectrum is propagated using horizon-crossing expansion rates and scale factors. Numerical backgrounds determine the present GW spectrum; broken-power-law sensitivity curves are used to assess experimental reach.

A broken-power-law template fitted to the numerical peak is tested against NANOGrav 15-year data with PTArcade. The analysis fixes σ = 6, ε = 0.25 and μ = −2, varies log10(Ab/s) and log10(fb/Hz), assumes Hellings–Downs correlations, and uses uniform priors [2,8] and [−10,−6], respectively.

The authors numerically evolve scalar and FLRW background equations, initially neglecting the potential. Appendix A obtains the initial Hubble rate by solving a quartic equation for the DBI Lorentz factor and selecting a real root of order unity.

Complexity is computed separately with the complexity-equals-volume prescription in the two-dimensional geometry. A time-translation conserved quantity E determines the extremal slice; its late-time critical value is reported as Ecrit = 1/zh.

The authors vary the bulk-plus-brane action to obtain bulk Einstein equations and Neumann boundary conditions, then evaluate extrinsic curvature and DGP-modified tension formulas. Appendix B dimensionally reduces the bulk theory along θ into a dilaton-gravity description.

Entropy calculations compare Hartman–Maldacena and static island extremal surfaces using area functionals. The former uses infalling Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates and conserved embedding quantities; the latter uses z(θ), perturbatively expanded Euler–Lagrange equations and brane Neumann conditions.

Adapts a triangle-diagram anomaly calculation normally presented with Pauli–Villars regularization. Here the authors introduce no auxiliary regulator, relying on claimed UV convergence from the nonlocal form factor; they also evaluate the required bubble contribution.

For Noether currents, expands derivative operators, isolates terms involving derivatives of the fermion field, then re-exponentiates and restores operator notation. The derivation uses on-shell photons to remove one contribution.

Contracts amplitudes with external momenta, evaluates γ-matrix traces and uses antisymmetry of the Levi-Civita tensor. Massive loop integrals are expressed through Feynman parameters and the exponential integral Ei.

The unbounded-entropy argument combines monotonicity with S(T)>log Z(T). Infinite-dimensionality makes Z(T) diverge as T increases without bound, under the assumed existence of the thermal partition function at every finite temperature.

For the mirror-curve scaling, analyze f(β)=∫₁∞exp(−βλ)log(λ)dλ/λ. The author uses a Mathematica Meijer G representation, a differential equation, and elementary bounds obtained by splitting the integral at λ=1/β. These arguments concern leading growth and, separately, a displayed series expansion.

Express the partition function as the Stieltjes integral Z=∫exp(−βλ)dN(λ), then use S=log Z+T∂T log Z. Imported large-energy counting asymptotics are the input for the high-temperature estimates, rather than an explicit computation of every eigenvalue.

Estimate mirror-electron freeze-out using dark-QED annihilation, neglecting its small Sommerfeld and bound-state corrections. Estimate colored freeze-out with QCD Sommerfeld factors, while treating subsequent bound-state formation as an important unresolved quantitative ingredient.

Integrate out singlet neutrinos to obtain visible, mirror, and mixed Weinberg operators. Mirror-neutrino lifetimes are estimated using heavy-neutral-lepton decay results; approximate entropy-injection formulas then determine dilution of dark relics and baryon asymmetry.

Compute an RG-improved two-loop Higgs effective potential and solve 4λeff+hλeff′=0. Iterative color matching and parity boundary conditions include mirror-quark thresholds with running up to three loops. The calculation uses tree-level color matching and neglects the two-loop top-Yukawa modification and mirror-electromagnetic running.

Match perturbations across the trigger-defined transition surface using Israel-type extrinsic-curvature matching. The quoted initial conditions are δτ*=−δq/q̄′, δρ/ρ̄=3ℋ*(1+w*)δτ*, and θ=−k²δτ*. Subsequent evolution uses synchronous-gauge fluid equations with vanishing viscosity.

Microscopic descriptions use semiclassical bounce-action estimates for vacuum tunneling and percolation, or a temperature-dependent gauge-scalar effective potential for Hot NEDE. These calculations relate transition timing and released vacuum energy to phenomenological parameters.

TriggerCLASS implements the phenomenological model in a Boltzmann solver. The reviewed MCMC analysis uses Planck CMB, BAO, and uncalibrated Pantheon supernovae, with an additional analysis imposing Gaussian distance-ladder H0 and weak-lensing S8 priors.

Expand the curvature action to quadratic order, introduce z=a√Qs and v=zR, and quantize Fourier modes satisfying vₖ″+(k²−z″/z)vₖ=0. Bogoliubov transformations and a Wronskian condition constrain the mode normalization.

Use MGCosmoMC to fit a truncated primordial spectrum to Planck 2018 results, then MGCAMB to calculate primordial, TT, EE, TE and matter spectra. Late-time modified gravity is represented by scale- and time-dependent μ(k,a) and γ(k,a).

Approximate z″/z using slow-roll parameters, solve the mode equation with Hankel functions, and use large-argument asymptotics plus βₖ(τᵢ)=0 to relate integration constants. The scalar spectrum follows from the two-point function.

Polar scalar parameterization produces a cosine potential for angular modes. Axial rephasings remove these modes from colored-fermion masses, trading them for derivative axial-current interactions and anomalous gluon/photon couplings.

Chiral field rephasings first express SM strong CP violation through θ̄. A further specified rotation of sector-2 fermions and ξ_2 is used to remove θ̄ simultaneously from the QCD term and dark scalar potential.
Solve corrected equations to first order in c_i using effective stress tensor ΔT and current ΔJ evaluated on leading backgrounds. Impose a constant static probe potential V_0=m_0√(−g_tt)−q_0 A_t.

Use two-center backgrounds inside a hierarchical three-black-hole system. An axial ansatz, far-zone inverse-radius expansion and Gegenbauer harmonics determine corrections through O(c_i,m_2 c_i); the monopole harmonic supplies the tightened constraints.

Alternative magnetic probes reproduce the electric three-body constraints when combined with electric two-body constraints: magnetic black holes in D=4 and parallel magnetic strings in D=5. The string construction also imposes removal of horizon logarithms.

Perturbative β-functions, anomalous dimensions and stability matrices through three loops; two-loop calculations use RGBeta, supplemented by general three-loop formulas. Composite-operator anomalous dimensions use the dummy-field method, including operator mixing.

Orbifold/orientifold projections relate planar diagrams after coupling rescaling. Padé approximants extrapolate ε expansions to d=3 and d=2; poles and crossings of operators with identical quantum numbers serve as reliability diagnostics.

Use differential-form backgrounds for continuous symmetries and triangulated cochains/cup products for discrete ones. Short exact sequences generate Bockstein maps; one explicit obstruction relation is δw2 = −Bock(B2e).

Geometric calculations use wrapped branes, relative-homology quotients and intersection numbers. The holographic example instead extracts topological equations by dimensional reduction of supergravity equations and Bianchi identities.

Compute screening equivalence classes of extended operators and take their Pontryagin duals. For U(1)^r with matter-charge lattice Qmatter, unscreened Wilson charges form Z^r/Qmatter; Smith normal form supplies a practical computation.
The theoretical discussion diagonalizes kinetic terms through the stated shift A′μ⇒A′μ+κBμ. It identifies induced χ couplings κe′cosθW to the photon and −κe′sinθW to the Z boson.

Search strategies include anomalously low ionization in scintillators or silicon, electron recoils in neutrino detectors, and missing-energy/momentum methods. The review compiles exclusion contours and simulation-based sensitivity projections rather than presenting a new discovery analysis.

Accelerator production mechanisms summarized are Drell–Yan pair production, direct vector-meson and quarkonium decays, pseudoscalar Dalitz decays, bremsstrahlung and photoproduction. A mixed-phase vector can additionally decay into two detector-traversing mCPs.

Use entropy-functional gradient flows for metric–scalar evolution. Perelman’s combined flow is presented as volume-preserving; generalized entropy functionals and field rescalings are then used to associate flows with actions.

Construct field-space lengths from Lagrangian kinetic terms and spacetime volume-normalised averages. Metric variations use a parameter-dependent DeWitt metric; varying the length functional gives geodesic equations, with particular attention to τ=0.

Solve stationarity equations together with V=Λ, eliminate the uplift coefficient, and eliminate other moduli to obtain a univariate critical-point polynomial. Gröbner bases are explicitly used for the model with one complex structure.

Rescale nonmonic polynomials while preserving their splitting fields; factor reducible cases and use discriminants, irreducibility criteria, relative resolvents and trimmed invariants in Stauduhar subgroup decision trees.

Magma is used for selected flux values, particularly the degree-34 case. The appendix describes modular factorization, p-adic root approximations and subsequent Stauduhar iteration as computational ingredients.

Extremality is obtained by simultaneous equality and tangency of the two curves, equivalently the double-root/zero-temperature condition. The authors derive critical normalizations ce and use small-c, or joint small-b and small-c, expansions of extremal charge-to-mass ratios.

Solve f(r)=0 after introducing v=1/r. Horizon candidates are intersections of yL=1−2Mv+Q²v² with yR=cv^(3ωq+1), or yR=b+cv^(3ωq+1). Graphical intersection counting supplies much of the evidence because the general root equation is described as complicated.

For equal kinetic mixing, diagonalize the permutation-symmetric kinetic matrix and rescale its eigenmodes to canonical normalization. Exact copies then have two mass classes; the unequal-mass single-YM example additionally requires diagonalization of the resulting mass matrix and evaluation of two-photon lifetimes.

Misalignment calculations retain homogeneous axion modes and the quadratic approximation to the periodic potential. Oscillations begin at ma=3H; visible-sector radiation sets the clock, and adiabatic conservation of comoving axion number propagates the density to the present.

Dilute-star analysis uses nonrelativistic Klein–Gordon reduction to Gross–Pitaevskii–Poisson equations, followed by a Madelung hydrodynamic transformation. Equal sector densities illustrate maximal collective effects, separating quantum pressure from attractive or repulsive self-interaction pressure.

Integrate out the massive axion at its minimum, then use thin-wall semiclassical Euclidean instantons between locally maximally symmetric backgrounds. O(4)-symmetric geometries are glued with gravitational junction conditions, and transition rates are estimated as Γ∼exp(−Sbounce). Several derivational details are delegated to earlier work.

Complete squares in the multi-flux energy and estimate lattice-point counts in thin shells of constant vacuum energy, restricted to an allowed flux box. The counting criterion asks for at least one state within an observationally acceptable energy interval; estimates assume comparable sector parameters and a restricted solid angle.

Repackage throat dynamics as two-dimensional JT dilaton gravity coupled to matter, then quantize its Schwarzian mode. Supersymmetric extremality requires additional light fermionic modes and JT supergravity.
Gravitational path integrals with asymptotic boundary conditions chosen for partition functions or probe correlators; light throat fluctuations require quantum treatment beyond the classical saddle.
Use KiDS-1000 weak-lensing auto- and cross-correlations across five tomographic bins through the COSEBIs likelihood. Predict the matter power spectrum using HMcode.

Sample parameters with CLASS+MontePython using Metropolis–Hastings, requiring Gelman–Rubin R−1<10⁻². Estimate relative Bayesian evidence with MCEvidence and interpret its magnitude using a revised Jeffreys scale.

Combine Planck 2018 temperature, polarization and lensing likelihoods with weakly model-dependent transverse BAO measurements from SDSS. Pantheon+ supplies 1701 light curves of 1550 distinct supernovae over z=0.001–2.26; separate fits include SH0ES Cepheid host-distance calibration.

Integrate energy injection over a continuous KK distribution, include delayed deposition through channel-dependent f-curves, and project deposition histories onto CMB principal components. The authors report agreement with ExoCLASS plus MontePython MCMC constraints.

Use modified DarkHistory evolution for ionization and IGM temperature. Galactic analyses integrate decay flux through a halo profile and compare binned INTEGRAL/NuSTAR observations; the 511 keV analysis instead limits total positron injection.

Compute redshift-integrated extragalactic photon flux including hydrogen photoionization attenuation. Use χ² likelihoods and Metropolis–Hastings sampling for conservative total-flux limits and stronger limits assuming astrophysics explains the measured background.

Construct oscillons through normal-mode/harmonic expansions and numerical space-time collocation. Construct boson stars by shooting between origin and boundary power-series expansions, matching the scalar derivative while solving for the oscillation frequency.

Compute vacuum-subtracted RT/HRT entropies. Boson-star stability is assessed through spherically symmetric linear perturbations and Chebyshev pseudospectral collocation; real mode frequencies indicate stability within this analysis.

Use Euclidean hemisphere path integrals and bulk-to-boundary propagators for leading coherent-state preparation. Separately, apply a weak-energy-condition differential inequality, Grönwall's theorem and RT surface comparison to bound entanglement.

Vary the Einstein–Hilbert action while retaining boundary contributions; adopt an extended Palatini identity and connection displacement δΓ^γ_{αβ}=(b/M_P)σ^γg_{αβ}. These geometrical prescriptions follow cited earlier work.

Fourier-expand scalar and tensor fields, integrate their mode equations numerically, and initialize ψ_k=aZ_k and α_k=aY_k using approximately de Sitter conformal-time equations with Bessel/Hankel solutions.

Analyzes Kerr–Schild components near the disk using r proportional to |z| locally. Near the ring, introduces toroidal coordinates x=(a+ρcosψ)cosφ, y=(a+ρcosψ)sinφ, z=ρsinψ, and examines metric, curvature and effective-matter limits as ρ→0.

Uses curvature invariants, a normalized null tetrad and an associated orthonormal frame to characterize the metric and diagonalize the Ricci tensor and effective stress tensor. The paper imports the Petrov-D characterization with repeated principal null directions l and n.
Numerically solve the linear growth equation δ″+(3/a+E′/E)δ′−3Ω_mδ/(2a⁵E²)=0, where E=H/H₀ and primes denote scale-factor derivatives. Form D(z)=δ(z)/δ(0).

Use the Sheth–Tormen halo mass function with A=0.322, a=0.707 and p=0.3, a real-space top-hat filter, and P(k,z)=P₀(k)T²(k)D²(z). A spherical-collapse calculation is reported to give δ_c≈1.686 at high redshift for all nine examples.

Map stellar to halo mass through M_⋆=ϵf_bM_halo and compute ρ_⋆(>M_⋆,z)=ϵf_b∫_{M_⋆/(ϵf_b)}^∞M(dn/dM)dM. Compare the resulting curves with the historically inferred CEERS candidate-galaxy stellar mass densities.

Crepant resolutions, compact thimble representatives, linking/intersection pairings, lattice saturation, and Smith normal forms compute charge quotients. Equivariant cohomology supplies an alternative method for non-Abelian torus quotients.

Mayer–Vietoris gluing of singular neighborhoods X_loc to their complement X° tracks defect completion and symmetry trivialization. For ADE K3, the key sequence is 0 → H_2(X°) → H_2(X) → H_1(∂X_loc) → H_1(X°) → 0; isolated threefold examples use paired degree-2 and degree-4 sequences.

Review estimates of chiral-GW anomaly condensates and one-loop integration of graviton fluctuations around approximately de Sitter backgrounds. Compare with renormalized matter-field calculations, then represent dominant graviton corrections by an effective R ln(R/R₀) action; detailed cosmological fits are delegated to earlier work.

Implement the anomaly-modified Bianchi identity by an axionic Lagrange multiplier in the path integral, then integrate out the Kalb–Ramond field strength. The displayed effective action is truncated at O(α′), with higher-derivative terms omitted.

The authors integrate the worldsheet partition function over the modular fundamental domain using q-expansions and charge-lattice sums. Numerical integration supplies vacuum energies and integrated partition-function Hessians; moduli dependence is organized through pR.

Primitive embeddings of root-lattice overlattices W into Γv determine left-moving gauge groups and their global form. Enumerating vectors in W* and the orthogonal-complement dual, followed by sector-membership checks, also captures tachyons with nonzero pR that overlattices alone miss.

Compares best-fit distance, distance-modulus and H(z) predictions and uncertainty-normalized residuals for selected dataset combinations. Appendix A extends inference to wCDM+Alens, with flat Alens prior [0,5], to test sensitivity to anomalous lensing smoothing.

Diagnoses Planck preferences by cutting low or high multipoles, separately retaining or excluding lowE. A reported CAMB test switches off the late ISW contribution and removes the low-multipole difference between the compared ΛCDM and wCDM best-fit spectra.

MCMC inference uses Cobaya with CAMB for most runs and Montepython with CLASS-PT for FS analyses. Chains are deemed converged at Gelman–Rubin R−1<0.02. Dataset nuisance parameters are marginalized, with many FS nuisance terms treated analytically.

The reconstruction uses a squared-exponential Gaussian process fitted to H(z) and E(z), sampling 10,000 histories at 1,000 redshifts over 0≤z≤2. Physicality cuts and alternative quantile constructions are compared.
Modified CLASS evolves background and field perturbations, propagating varying α through recombination. MontePython MCMC uses a Gelman–Rubin convergence requirement |R−1|<0.05.

Vary gravitational/scalar actions to obtain background equations; decompose linear perturbations into scalar, vector and tensor sectors; use Fourier modes, power spectra and model-dependent evolution indices to express nS, nT and r.

Determine inflation's endpoint from ε1=1, integrate N=∫Hdt, and express horizon-crossing observables through model parameters. Compare parameter choices with quoted Planck constraints. A separate reconstruction procedure prescribes H(N) and solves a differential equation for f(R).

Schwinger proper-time representations turn one-loop determinants and effective actions into phase-space integrals. The finite-temperature extension uses Matsubara sums; proper-time integration is deferred until the end.
Modular regularization restricts phase-space lattice sums to finitely many cells: N=(NpNq)^4 and l^4 MΛ^4=Nℏ^4. A phase-space-volume estimate is then combined with a gravitational entropy bound.

Linearizes around smeared solutions and solves Poisson equations for localization corrections. Estimates Green functions analytically and numerically, then combines geometric diameter/volume/eigenvalue bounds with flux quantization, tadpole cancellation and anomaly constraints.

Combines dilaton and Einstein equations, dimensional reduction to the universal dilaton/volume potential, and dilaton stability. For dS/Minkowski the analysis imposes ∂τ²V>0; these universal-sector conditions are necessary, not sufficient for existence or full stability.

Solves supersymmetric conditions for two Kähler moduli using Lambert W branches, adds a D-term, minimizes in the remaining modulus and performs canonical normalization. Cosmological predictions use the cited microscopic k-space treatment of first-order perturbations.

Uses the N=1 supergravity F-term formula with corrected K and a two-exponential superpotential. The authors compute expressions in Mathematica 12, then separate perturbative, nonperturbative and mixed contributions in a large-volume expansion.

Uses embedding-coordinate geodesic lengths d = R arccosh ζ, explicit intersections of bulk null surfaces with Q, and connected/disconnected HRT candidate comparisons. Geometric arguments combine null-membrane focusing, causal-wedge inclusion, and maximin.
Reviews holographic quantum tasks: parallel B84 tasks and teleportation relate successful bulk scattering to necessary boundary mutual information, motivating connected entanglement wedges.

Higher gauging sums networks of discrete q-form symmetry defects along a codimension-p submanifold, producing a condensation defect without changing the bulk theory. It requires p-gaugeability and p≤q+1; the p=q+1 construction is a non-simple projection-type defect. Condensation defects act trivially on local operators.

Modular S covariance relates a symmetry insertion in a torus trace to a defect-twisted Hilbert space. Requiring non-negative integer character multiplicities constrains candidate Ising symmetry operators. Arf-weighted sums over spin structures implement bosonization and its inverse.

Half gauging introduces discrete BF gauge theory on one side of an interface, with Dirichlet boundary condition a|=0. This gives a topological interface between T and T/G; when gauging is followed by an isomorphism back to T, it yields an internal duality defect. A particular discrete-torsion choice is used.
Uses naive dimensional analysis for poorly known three-pion and four-nucleon couplings, explores contact-coupling sign choices, and compares EDM ratios under alternative dominant-source hypotheses.

Integrates out heavy BSM fields and electroweak fields, matches dimension-six operators onto low-energy CP-odd operators, and applies one-loop RG evolution with quark thresholds down to approximately 1 GeV.

Uses published QCD sum-rule estimates for nucleon EDMs, chiral-symmetry relations and sum-rule inputs for pion-nucleon couplings, and imported nuclear/atomic response coefficients. These are theoretical inputs rather than independently established normalizations.

GaPP reconstructs H(z) and redshift derivatives using squared-exponential, Cauchy and Matérn ν = 9/2 kernels. Kernels are chosen manually; hyperparameters are selected through the GP marginal likelihood.

Friedmann and conservation equations provide scalar density and pressure, hence V = (ρφ − Pφ)/2. The gradient reconstruction uses dV/dφ = (dV/dz)/(dφ/dz), φ̇ = −(1+z)H dφ/dz and φ̇² = ρφ + Pφ. Here 'model-independent' means no specified scalar potential or dark-energy parameterization.

Integrates the projection of −∇log m along unit-speed geodesics to obtain exponential mass bounds. Uses convex-hull projections and Poincaré-half-plane geodesics with rational endpoints to relate local charge bounds to infinite-distance behavior.

Computes α-vectors by local canonical normalization and differentiation of string tensions or BPS masses. In nine dimensions, combines the volume direction with axio-dilaton geodesics and evaluates KK/winding projections along them.
Reviews matrix-integral saddle-point and anomaly-based effective-field-theory treatments of the supersymmetric Cardy limit, followed by a Legendre transform to obtain large-angular-momentum entropy.

Orthogonalizes flavor currents by Gram-Schmidt, constructs convex hulls from extreme charge-to-dimension vectors of chiral gauge-invariant operators, and evaluates their minimum distance from the origin.
Uses anomaly cancellation to identify flavor symmetries and determine R-charges where possible; otherwise applies a-maximization to obtain superconformal R-charges and anomaly central charges.

Uses Poisson summation and Fourier-Bessel expansions for numerical surface scans. In D=8, matches the one-loop string amplitude to a dimensionally regularized supergravity box integral to fix the finite subtraction convention.

Constructs fundamental domains recursively using Iwasawa coordinates, successive maximal abelian parabolic subgroups, primitive lattice vectors and quadratic constraints, generalizing Grenier's construction.
Constrains Taylor expansions by finite stabilizer groups. Counts invariant quadratic polynomials to reduce Hessian tests to a Laplacian criterion or a small number of second derivatives.
Uses an effective-operator model to connect Higgs–dark-matter mixing and decay with the energy bias between domain-wall vacua, rather than deriving either effect from a specified compactification.
Maps previously reported CMB lifetime constraints and radio-decay sensitivity estimates into bounds and forecasts for ΛQG, using electromagnetic energy injection from dark-matter decays.

Uses radiation-era wall-annihilation estimates and a broken-power-law gravitational-wave spectrum. The low-frequency slope is a=3 by causality; simulations motivate b≈c≈1. Detector prospects are plotted using SNR=10.

Review of pole-subtracted amplitude expansions and dispersive sum rules: deform a low-energy contour to UV discontinuities, use the optical theorem, and remove the residue at infinity with Froissart growth assumptions.

Expand coefficient functions around a scalar vacuum to relate elastic scattering and Higgs-associated production. The illustrative collider estimates use angular distributions and event-count statistical projections; toy-model matching uses Matchete.

Count M2-brane states from collapsing fibral curves: organize covering-algebra roots into monodromy orbits, compute weights by intersections, and use Riemann–Hurwitz to determine branched-curve genera and multiplicities. Shioda-type divisors determine Abelian charges.

Engineer singularities by generalized Tate vanishing orders of line-bundle sections; resolve using toric tops and Stanley–Reisner data; construct polynomial Jacobian maps and inspect leading Weierstrass coefficients.

Use Batyrev polytope formulas for Hodge numbers and non-polynomial deformations. Compare geometric transitions with Coulomb/Higgs-branch state counting, and use LST 2-group structure constants as duality consistency tests.

Estimate average information emission by dividing Bekenstein–Hawking entropy by evaporation time, then compare it with the entropy equivalent of Bekenstein’s maximum bit-transfer rate. Repeat the comparison over a short interval corresponding to a single emitted quantum.

Consider a phenomenological power-law family dM/dt=−λ(mPl/tPl)(mPl/M)^n with 0≤n<2, and compare the resulting information inequality with the Penrose inequality. A later smooth interpolation is used to describe the transition between conventional and constant-rate regimes.

Obtain interior equations by the stated signature-changing continuation, giving M̃(f̃)=−iM(−if̃) and P̃(f̃)=−1+∫₀ᶠ̃M̃(u)du. Track square-root branches and contours to determine coordinate patches and whether their endpoints occur at finite or infinite proper time.

Use the Gasperini–Veneziano parametrization: invert f(M)=F′(M) locally, prescribe M(f), and obtain metric, dilaton and coordinate through quadratures. Define g(f)=∫₀ᶠM(u)du and P(f)=1−g(f); real exterior solutions require P≥0.

Summing Kloosterman residues selects only Rademacher index ℓ=1 for K and A, and ℓ=2 for M. These terms recover the S and P transformations connecting dual channels; explicit model calculations also use Chan–Paton coefficients and tadpole constraints.

Exact character degeneracies are expressed through the circle/Rademacher method, modified Bessel functions and generalized Kloosterman sums. Refining by periodic residue classes and continuing the level variable defines enveloping functions and sector averaged sums.

Bulk–brane interactions hᵢⱼ Lᵢ H̃ Ψⱼ(y=0), followed by canonical KK-mode normalization, give bulk-volume suppression of four-dimensional Yukawa couplings. An approximate rewriting explicitly drops factors of π and the string coupling.

Oscillation calculations use a unitary 3+1 mixing matrix U = U₃₄ U₂₄ U₁₄ UPMNS and Hamiltonian H = U M² U†/(2E), followed by a short-baseline reduction and comparison of electron-neutrino disappearance spectra.

Gauge charge conjugation in the minimal Abelian defect theories AN,p, examine the resulting time-reversal symmetry and anomaly indicators, and vary symmetry fractionalization. Characteristic-class and Wu-structure actions identify the anomalies being matched.

Represent generalized FS data by bulk SPT phases with decorated domain walls. Test whether the duality-defect TQFT supplies the worldvolume time-reversal anomaly needed to cancel the domain-wall endpoint anomaly through a compatible non-invertible extension.

Use the symmetry-TQFT interval construction with a polarization boundary and a physical boundary. Analyze loop condensation through g-invariant Lagrangian subgroups; trivial intersection with the electric polarization is additionally required for an invertible absolute boundary theory.

For two Narain partition functions, either unfold the factors successively or use their product as a central-charge-2c Narain partition function. The latter reduces the computation to the Eisenstein-overlap machinery through its pole contribution.

Insert the Eisenstein Fourier expansion and perform Gaussian and Bessel integrals. Organize nondegenerate orbits by invariant 2×2 minors Dᵢⱼ, enumerate consistent integral representatives, and evaluate the degenerate contribution using the imported Epstein-zeta recursion.

Apply an imported unfolding method to the Poisson-resummed Narain lattice sum. Decompose lattice coordinates into SL(2,Z) orbits; stabilizers equal to Γ∞ or the identity turn fundamental-domain integrals into strip or upper-half-plane integrals.

Solve large-N Schwinger–Dyson equations with an infrared power-law propagator after dropping the free inverse propagator. Extract exchanged dimensions from ladder-kernel eigenvalues satisfying k(Δ,ℓ)=1; the boundary theory first has a coupled matrix kernel.

Expand four-point functions in conformal partial waves, use shadow symmetry and a Sommerfeld–Watson-like complex-spin contour deformation, then analytically continue to the OTOC second sheet. Compare momentum saddle contributions with pole residues in Regge and light-cone limits.

Construct the free bulk propagator by images and Fourier transform parallel to the boundary. Boundary central-charge data are extracted from stress-tensor OPE residues; hyperbolic chaos follows from the Regge intercept.

Use a toric reflexive-polytope construction and the Batyrev formula to obtain Hodge numbers. A quartic fiber equation, Stanley–Reisner ideal and restrictions to divisors identify fibral components and their monodromy.

Shrink the g1 fiber component, then apply the Jacobian map to obtain Weierstrass coefficients. The displayed leading discriminant is Δ = f1^6 D4,Z + O(f1^7); its fiber interpretation is used to infer the Jacobian gauge symmetry.

Interpret monodromy through foldings of affine Dynkin diagrams, and infer gauge rank from fibral divisors. The review also describes the elliptic divisor decomposition into pulled-back base divisors, fibral divisors, the zero-section and free Mordell–Weil generators.

Extract relational volume and matter dynamics from operator averages; Fourier transform rod variables, solve volume equations analytically with Bessel functions, and compare numerical matter and curvature-like solutions with GR.

Take expectation values of GFT equations on linearized perturbed coherent peaked states. Gaussian peaking permits derivative expansions, truncated at first order in the small temporal and spatial width parameters.

For independent exponent vectors, use the Gram matrix Aij = αi · αj and the reviewed scaling formula p = Σij (A⁻¹)ij. Combine imported stability results with asymptotic dominance arguments that discard subleading exponentials.
Track universal volume and string-coupling powers of flux, curvature and source contributions. Bound the potential-gradient parameter using the τ derivative and positivity of retained contributions.

Rotate canonical scalar fields to factorize the potential as exp(α′1 φ′1) U(transverse fields). Scaling rolls along φ′1 while the transverse fields sit at a critical point; stability additionally requires a positive transverse Hessian of U.

Extend the modular numerical framework to search directly for scalar-potential extrema instead of solving DIW=0. The stated minimum criterion includes positive definiteness of the Hessian after locating critical points.

Randomize flux vectors and initial moduli guesses. ISD± initialization tends to converge rapidly to F-flat minima and is avoided for the non-F-flat search. For the flagship comparison, both classes use the same uniform sampling and equal sample sizes.

Reconstruct bilinear pieces through contractions with the explicit toroidal metric, volume tensors and four-cycle volumes. Epsilon contractions replace mixed-tensor prime fluxes by computationally simpler index representations, with explicit 1/4! and 1/6! factors.
Compute the F-term potential from K and W using V=e^K(K^{I J̄} D_I W D_J̄ W̄−3|W|²), then classify its terms by pairs of flux species. The full W is linear in S and cubic in both the T and U sectors.

Introduce 128 axionic flux combinations polynomial in the RR C0 and C4 axions. The authors describe invertible linear relations between ordinary and axionic flux components at specified axions, absorbing explicit RR-axion dependence into these combinations.

The appendix separately counts tower states below the species scale, uses Λ_sp = M_p/√N, and evaluates the corresponding mass-truncated sum by Euler–Maclaurin expansion. The paper compares this cylindrical cutoff prescription with its main five-dimensional momentum cutoff.

The authors evaluate a Euclidean one-loop logarithmic determinant with a finite KK sum constrained jointly with four-momentum by a five-dimensional cutoff. They integrate over four-momentum and apply the Euler–Maclaurin formula, retaining its remainder to identify UV-insensitive terms.

Compute canonically normalized masses from the potential Hessian using primitive/non-primitive metric decompositions and compare with the AdS BF bound. Test selected membrane nucleation channels through charges and tensions of appropriately oriented D2/D6 configurations.

Use the flux-axion bilinear potential V=Z^{AB}ρAρB, with saxion-dependent Z, to solve axion and saxion extremization equations. Additional branches arise when coefficient brackets vanish separately, avoiding a proportionality condition imposed in an earlier classification.

For fixed-base elliptic fibrations, solve the vacuum equations perturbatively in εA=cA/mA around the factorised solution. Numerical solutions in two explicit two- and three-Kähler-parameter models test the expansion and its mass-spectrum predictions.
Separate the charged Klein-Gordon equation using spherical harmonics and frequency or momentum modes; solve the resulting ordinary differential equations with Gauss hypergeometric functions.

Apply Riemann P-function monodromy connection formulas as a second calculation of the mean numbers. Use complex phase-integral contours and horizon-pole residues to interpret their leading exponential factors.

Use in-out Bogoliubov coefficients with different boundary prescriptions: zero incoming flux at the cosmological horizon for inner tunneling, and zero initial negative-frequency mode for outer time scattering. The respective mean-number ratios are |T|²/|R|² and |R|²/|I|².
Combine the wavelength-based static inequality with the maximum excitation energy, then impose positive pressures and bounded asymptotic curvature. An assumed A(r)=Cr^k form is restricted to k=2.
Local typicality estimates s(r)∼4πr²ρ(r)/ϵ(r). The Hamiltonian constraint a′=8πGr²ρ introduces self-gravity and makes entropy a functional of the self-consistent geometry.

Use the local Unruh temperature and radial one-dimensional Gibbs relation to determine entropy density. Entropy-current conservation and Gauss’ theorem relate the spatial entropy integral to an ingoing light-sheet integral.

Smith normal decomposition determines periodicity-lattice bases and fundamental-domain volumes. Minima are selected by positive-definite Hessians after diagonal rescaling that preserves inertia and mitigates the extreme coefficient hierarchies.

Amplitude-ordered truncation retains N independent charge rows and sufficiently large dependent contributions, using a relative threshold t. A linear coordinate change separates most axion directions; a Python root finder treats the reduced coupled system, starting from approximately 10^5 uniformly sampled points in its fundamental domain.

CYTools generates geometries using random triangulations: 1,000 distinct geometries at each sampled h^{1,1}≥4, and the maximum available for smaller values, across N=1–491. Moduli start at the stretched Kähler-cone tip and are dilated to satisfy the additional control criterion.

Treat E1=0 as a Hamiltonian constraint preserved by the evolution equations. Analyze its concave quadratic in X=e^{-2f}, then numerically integrate a three-dimensional flow in (dot f,H,X), eliminating spatial-scale variable Z through the constraint.

Construct internal gauge fields from torsion-free spin connections using ’t Hooft symbols and so(4)=su(2)+⊕su(2)−. The imported Einstein-manifold construction removes mixed Hodge-curvature blocks, yielding self-dual and anti-self-dual field strengths; F^i∧F^i tests density uniformity.

Super-Weyl gauge fixing, matter and ghost superconformal anomalies, and the proposed gravitational measure Jacobian reduce the quantum problem to super-Liouville path integrals divided by residual super-Moebius volumes.

Semiclassical saddle expansions use spherical harmonics, heat-kernel determinants, and two-loop propagator diagrams. N = 2 localization instead uses Q-exact deformations; its deformation-independence argument requires a Q-invariant measure and absence of field-space boundary contributions.

First-order BPS equations are solved using successive scalar redefinitions, a conserved dilatonic quantity j, an auxiliary coordinate Y, and integration constants k and a. Root and discriminant analysis classifies regularity. The remaining dilaton integral is evaluated numerically rather than analytically.

Near-boundary BPS expansions identify sources and condensates. Adding the Gibbons–Hawking term permits rewriting the action as squared BPS equations plus a total derivative; a supersymmetric flat-boundary counterterm cancels that derivative.

Two further approaches address the conformal factor problem: a hypothetical nonlinear extension of Gibbons-Hawking-Perry contour rotation, and a Lorentzian fixed-area prescription producing integrals over Euclidean fixed-area saddles. Minimal cuts and suitable boundary/corner terms support sewing additivity.

Reflect, cut and reglue dominant saddles to construct configurations for the separate traces. Action additivity, monotonicity under reflection identifications and minimization give I(σBC) ≥ I(σB)+I(σC). In the classically saturated case, perturbative bulk Hilbert-space positivity controls quantum corrections.

In the Saad-Shenker-Stanford treatment of JT, integrate the dilaton along imaginary values to impose R = −2. Reduce the remaining gravitational action to boundary Schwarzian actions and use their lower bounds together with nonnegative matter action.

Generalized Scherk-Schwarz Ansätze in SO(8,8) Exceptional Field Theory uplift the gauged-supergravity family to NSNS fields. Embedding into SO(8,24) captures heterotic vector perturbations; embedding into E8(8) extends the type II treatment to RR fields and fermionic partners.

Expand fluctuations in scalar harmonics of the maximally symmetric S3 × T4 reference geometry. Twist-weighted derivatives act through representation matrices, turning linearized ExFT equations into algebraic mass matrices after removal of redundancies and Goldstone modes.

Identify deformations through commuting holomorphic/antiholomorphic currents in the SL(2,R)×SU(2)×U(1)^4 WZW worldsheet model, and through an orbifold-invariant sum of current products in the conjectured SymN(T4) boundary theory.

Numerical complex-time boundary-value solutions tune the South Pole scalar value to reach specified final scale factor and field values. Allowability is tested by whether the endpoint can be reached below the maximal Σ = π curve.

Friedmann evolution tracks curvature through inflation, radiation domination and matter domination. An adopted observational curvature bound determines minimum inflation; subsequent expansion converts the nucleation size into a present-size estimate.

Matches higher-dimensional equations and Bianchi identities to lower-dimensional cosmological equations, followed by consistent single-scalar subtruncations. Consistency establishes uplift of retained solutions, rather than completeness of the light spectrum.

Constructs late-time power-series, logarithmic and oscillatory-in-log(t) asymptotic solutions near P1, then numerically continues trajectories to examine their earlier evolution and acceleration intervals.

Uses an expansion-normalized phase plane and the Jacobian trace, determinant and discriminant to classify fixed points. The first Friedmann equation is imposed as a separate constraint, retaining the curvature information.

The perturbative argument integrates out fermions and uses explicit SU(3) dimensions, Dynkin indices and triality to establish an integrality condition representation by representation. The nonzero-triality case reduces to divisibility by 36 and elementary congruence cases.

The nonperturbative argument constructs correlated color and electromagnetic fluxes on a four-torus with twisted boundary conditions. Their normalized integrals are ∫tr(G∧G)/(8π²)=2/3 and ∫F∧F/(8π²)=1; axion periodicity then constrains the path-integral phase.

Extracts uplift and tower-volume/warping dependence from the throat metric and induced brane metric, then translates mass inequalities into constraints on conifold moduli and flux parameters. Species-scale and Regge-trajectory comparisons are ancillary estimates.

Reviews SO(1,4) unitary representations and a Casimir-based dS mass convention, m²=(s−q)(s+q−1)H². The subsequent bounds combine a working Higuchi inequality with the AdS vacuum-energy relation, tower scaling and the assumed gravitino hierarchy.

For difficult nonlinear evolution, mode-by-mode solutions use the GEF background to reconstruct bilinears. A self-correction procedure reinitializes higher-order bilinears when the consistency discrepancy exceeds a selected threshold, illustrated with 1%.
Linear perturbation theory uses Whittaker background modes and their retarded Green function. A power-law ansatz δϕ∝(−τ)^(−ζ) turns the memory-kernel equation into a numerical root problem.

The gradient expansion formalism (GEF) evolves a truncated hierarchy of electric, magnetic and mixed bilinears with increasing spatial derivatives. The newly linearized GEF reduces constant-background stability to eigenvalues of a constant-coefficient matrix.

The holographic calculation uses an information metric built from integrated two-point correlators of Lagrangian deformations, pulls it back along the RG flow, and normalizes elementary lengths by √C_T to express bulk distances in Planck units.

First-order BPS gradient-flow equations reduce single-step lengths to integrals involving |∂|Z||. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz and reverse-Hölder inequalities, including a q→∞ limit, produce bounds with endpoint-integral factors and residual profile dependence.

Schwinger–Keldysh diagrammatics uses spectator Wightman functions built from Bogoliubov-transformed modes. Each propagator is decomposed into the BD term, a reversed-frequency term and two anomalous-frequency terms, with their respective Bogoliubov weights.

Large-mass Gamma-function asymptotics diagnose exponential suppression. Three-point seeds are obtained through the single folded limit k4→0 of the four-point seeds, then examined in squeezed momentum configurations.

Time integrals are organized as scalar seed integrals. Bootstrap differential equations follow from propagator equations and integration by parts; collapsed-limit asymptotics fix integration constants. Homogeneous hypergeometric solutions carry oscillatory signals, while the particular solution supplies background.

Use magnetic line operators and discrete flux ω∈H²(M,Zp) to determine fractional instanton numbers through the Pontryagin square. Enforce invariance under the axion's full period for every allowed bundle to obtain coupling selection rules.

Compute embedding indices from representation branching, c=Σi T(Ri)/T(R), and match axion coefficients across Higgsing. Compare ultraviolet and infrared Fourier modes to identify small-instanton contributions absent from the infrared potential.

Use Euclidean bounce actions with Γ∼exp(−Sbounce). Eliminate square roots through junction conditions, then eliminate Λin and the nucleation radius to factorize the action before taking asymptotic limits. Compare the resulting regimes with electric and magnetic WGC inequalities.

Legendre/Routhian dualization replaces the 4-form by λ. The shifted 4-form is integrated out, a flux-independent term is absorbed into ΛQFT, and membrane charge, tension and gravitational boundary terms supply the junction conditions.

Reduce topological, potential and duality sectors separately using shifted currents, section constraints and cocycle identities. Projecting out Σ-only trivial parameters gives a Dorfman product satisfying an exact Leibniz identity; shifted Maurer–Cartan equations organise the topological term.
Generalised Scherk–Schwarz factorisation uses |Λ⟩=r⁻¹U⁻¹|λ⟩, VExFT(x,y)=V(x)U(y), and ρ=ϱr. A Weitzenböck connection and an additional constrained bra ⟨w+| determine the embedding tensor.

Autonomous-system methods include an IDE density system in e-folding time, eigenvalue and positive-density restrictions, and normalized exponential-quintessence variables. A dominant-balance truncation is introduced for the latter.

Auxiliary-field reconstruction writes F(R)=P(φ(R))R+Q(φ(R)). Choosing φ=t converts a prescribed expansion history into differential equations for P and Q, followed by auxiliary-field elimination when possible.
Hamilton–Jacobi reconstruction expresses H and the scalar potential in terms of the scalar field. The illustrated Type I/III histories use phantom fields; Type II/IV/V examples use nonphantom fields.

Non-standard couplings are constructed by changing SL(2,Z) frame, adding an integer-quantized θF′∧F′ interaction, and transforming back. The appendix instead maps generalized Maxwell equations to a closed field strength and requires their monodromy matrix to lie in SL(2,Z).
The standard quantization argument uses integral magnetic flux, the even intersection pairing on spin four-manifolds, and invariance of the exponentiated Euclidean action under θ→θ+2π.

Locally defining the magnetic dual potential away from sources yields AM→AM+A under a unit axion winding. Anomaly inflow on charged worldlines supplies localized degrees of freedom that implement the associated dyon spectrum.

Retain the exponential dependence on internal loop momentum and expand in small external momenta divided by Λ. The calculation explicitly restricts itself to leading order in this external-momentum expansion.

Apply the imported Non-locality Renormalization Scheme: subtract quadratic dependence on Λ and optionally logarithmic-like Ei dependence. Fourier-transform the dressed photon propagator for the potential and use first-order perturbation theory with local hydrogen wavefunctions for energy shifts.
Use Wick rotation, Feynman parameters, Dirac algebra, and Ward and Gordon identities to extract vertex form factors. A photon mass mγ regulates the ordinary logarithmic infrared divergence.

The reported string prescription performs Poisson resummation before subtracting the infinite radius-independent zero-mode contribution. The authors relate this procedure to modular invariance and compare it with finite-temperature and Casimir calculations.

The note examines parametric scaling rather than presenting a new loop computation: it substitutes R=1/mKK into two imported vacuum-energy expressions and compares species-scale and KK-scale choices of the UV cutoff.

Configuration-row conditions and triple intersections identify candidate limits. GV data are taken from a public database or computed using the cited Mathematica code, and inspected through degree ten.

The coupling analysis combines eigenvalue asymptotics of the gauge kinetic matrix with proper scalar distance computed from the same cubic prepotential. Circle reduction of a six-dimensional theory supplies the comparison scalings for KK particles and string oscillator modes.

The spectral diagnostic compares bounded, possibly periodic GV indices at increasing KK charge with exponential growth expected for charged string states. Periodicity allows projections by discrete symmetries or orbifold actions rather than requiring identical multiplicities at every charge.

Use the effective-action flow ∂tΓk=(1/2)Tr[Gk∂tRk], with Gk=(Γk^(0,2)+Rk)⁻¹. A Callan-Symanzik spectral cutoff Rk=Zφk² preserves causality and Lorentz invariance but requires flowing counterterms; only the combined renormalized flow is finite.

The reviewed Standard Model computation feeds running parameters back into their flows, expands the Higgs potential about its flowing minimum, includes external functional-QCD input in the strong infrared regime, and determines the top pole through its complex-momentum two-point function.

Expand in fluctuation vertices and momentum-dependent tensor dressings. The infinite fluctuation hierarchy drives mixed and background vertices; finite fluctuation order does not close without approximation. At k=0, STI-compatible vertices can be mapped to curvature form factors.

Algebraic quantization, point-split stress tensors and Hadamard subtraction define difference QEIs relative to a reference Hadamard state. Positivity of differentiated two-point functions bounds the state-independent contribution; derivatives of the smearing function isolate a Wick-square contribution.

Conformal metric transformations and scalar redefinitions relate frames. Quantum arguments examine the resulting functional Jacobian and Euclidean constrained instantons fixing the zero mode of ϕ² through a Lagrange multiplier.

Evaluate BPS Schwinger integrals in a graviphoton background, using the Gopakumar–Vafa representation. For a rigid S², sum D2–D0 central charges over all integer D0 charges; perform the proper-time integral before regulating infinite sums with Riemann ζ-functions. An alternative uses Hurwitz ζ-functions.

Use heterotic/IIA duality and modular constraints on the heterotic one-loop prepotential. The map T1→T and T2→4πS identifies the IIA terms with heterotic tree, one-loop and nonperturbative contributions.

Count the evenly spaced D0 tower through Nsp=ΛIIA/mD0 and solve the ten-dimensional species relation. Apply IIA/M-theory duality to reinterpret D0, D2 and NS5 constituents as circle momentum and transverse M-branes.

Use BPS brane tensions to assign mp∼Tp^(1/(p+1)), express these scales relative to the species cutoff and inverse species number, and identify towers that remain parametrically at or below the cutoff.

A Schwinger-proper-time representation motivates a proposed light-cone continuation: evaluate Lorentzian momentum integrals for ℓ_E² > 0, then continue their results to ℓ_E² = −iℓ². This preserves Lorentzian spacetime signature while changing the length parameter.

Extract the outgoing Wightman function using light-cone ordering, infer a Fourier-mode operator algebra, and calculate wave-packet particle numbers using Bogoliubov coefficients. Finite-duration detection is represented by a switching function s(v).

Appendix A compares Ryu–Takayanagi geodesic segments with horizon shadows. For the joined conformal-fluid brane, numerically solve for Z(g) and energy density rather than g(Z), impose regularity at the tip, and obtain the second half by reflection.

Vary the gravitational action with unfixed induced brane metric to obtain junction conditions. Use an ADM decomposition adapted to the brane embedding x=Lg(z), solve the constant-tension embedding, and transform its induced metric into JT black-hole form.

The natural nondegenerate pairing identifies V^C(Σ̂) with End(V^C(Σ)). Diagonal mapping class action becomes conjugation; Schur’s lemma makes the invariant subspace one-dimensional under irreducibility. Invariance of the pairing then establishes nonvanishing of an average with d_Σ(x) ≠ 0.

For property F, construct a finite invariant spanning set using plus/minus combinations of 1- and ε-colored basis vectors, rescalings, and powers of the order-16 twist. A linear transformation preserving this spanning set acts faithfully as a permutation of a finite set.

For Ising irreducibility, compute Dehn-twist, S-transformation and pure-braid actions in an admissible fusion-graph coloring basis. Twist projectors and label-changing mapping classes generate elementary matrices, yielding the full endomorphism algebra.

Specify an even unimodular Narain lattice, independent left/right lattice automorphisms, Spin lifts, and rational shifts. Determine untwisted and twisted spectra using invariant lattices and their duals, mass formulas, and level matching N(H_L,m−H_R,m)∈Z.

Apply 6d Green–Schwarz anomaly factorization and gauge-kinetic positivity; analyze maximal Higgsing by representation branching. Match resulting spectra to candidate geometric Hodge data, then use circle Wilson lines and Coulomb branches to obtain lower-dimensional spectra.
Decompose Γ into Levi-Civita connection, contortion and disformation. With torsion absent, use R(Γ)=R(g)+Q+Dα(Qα−Q̄α); imposing flatness and dropping the divergence constructs the STEGR action.

Use independent metric/connection variation in a Palatini formulation, with weight-one Lagrange multiplier densities enforcing flatness and zero torsion; alternatively vary the metric and four functions parametrizing the restricted connection.

Apply Lie-derivative symmetry reduction to both metric and connection. For quadratic extensions, use ADM decomposition and kinetic-matrix degeneracy to classify primary constraints; these classifications do not complete the physical mode count.

Study four classes: a common coordinate-dependent diagonal F; independent F1(a,Pa), F2(ϕ,Pϕ); a common fully phase-space-dependent diagonal F; and cross-coordinate momentum brackets. Slow-roll estimates are supplemented by the exact ansatz a=a0e^{Ht}; non-diagonal examples require additional momentum and exponential-function ansätze.

Replace brackets according to the proposed quantum commutators, solve the resulting velocity-momentum relations, and substitute into the constraint. General momentum-dependent functions require coupled inversions, so a universal explicit Friedmann equation is unavailable.

Dimensionally reduce the string-frame action and Weyl-rescale to four-dimensional Einstein frame. Require every contribution to the scalar potential to have the same N-scaling, solving for dilaton and subvolume exponents in terms of the independent F₄ exponents.

Estimate direction-dependent KK masses from the first Fourier mode of the dilaton. Expand a probe anti-D4 DBI action to obtain an open-string metric, then use field redefinitions to express the distance problem as geodesics on H²×R³.

Construct canonical momenta and a Hamiltonian, convert proper-time evolution to coordinate-time equations dr/dt and dπ_r/dt, and linearize them about π_r=0 and dπ_r/dt=0. The Lyapunov exponent is obtained from eigenvalues of the resulting 2×2 Jacobian.

Numerically solve for equilibrium radii and evaluate λ²−κ² while varying angular momentum and selected background parameters. Tables and figure captions provide orbital radii, angular-momentum thresholds, and exterior radial intervals.

Solve the axion response to V(a)+U(a)n(r) using local potential minima and an adiabatic approximation. A narrow surface region of width ℓ is then used to integrate the dilaton equation and obtain a jump in its radial derivative.

Minimize the combined interior axion/dilaton gradient energy and exterior dilaton energy over an integration constant, equivalently ϕ0, ϕ∞ or the surface value ϕs. The exterior contribution is 2πMp²L²/R. Exponential W and W² near a quadratic minimum are examined separately.
Cut and glue compact rimmed source manifolds, define ⟨N₁|N₂⟩=ζ(M_{N₁* N₂}), quotient null vectors, and complete. Gluing at the left or right boundary defines opposite surface-algebra actions.
Antisymmetrize states constructed from n copies of a projection using permutations of left-boundary labels. Positivity of their recursively computed norms enforces integer trace normalization.
Use higher-boundary Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities to bound surface operators; take weak/strong operator closures. Extend the trace on positive operators through tr(a)=sup_{β>0}⟨C̃β|a|C̃β⟩.

Match light-quark interactions to ChPT, diagonalize the quadratic ALP–meson Lagrangian, and supplement it with phenomenological vector, scalar, tensor and anomalous interactions. Compute decay amplitudes and widths in a Mathematica notebook; implement the revised phenomenology in SensCalc.

Solve previously developed RG equations through electroweak and lower-energy evolution, including diagonal and flavor-changing couplings. Heavy-quark couplings are frozen below their respective mass thresholds.

Obtain additional B-decay channels by rescaling transition results based on light-cone QCD sum rules for the corresponding FCNC operator. Generate leading-order gluon and quark fusion with FeynRules/MadGraph5 using NNPDF 3.1 NNLO PDFs.
Worldline one-loop graviton amplitudes, followed by Poisson resummation of KK momentum, generate the relevant R2 and R4 structures and isolate a divergent zero-winding contribution.

Special geometry and quantum attractor equations encode supersymmetric higher-derivative F-terms through a generalized prepotential F(X,Υ), with coefficients supplied by topological-string amplitudes.

An AdS2×S8 near-horizon ansatz defines an entropy function by Legendre transformation in the electric field. General curvature terms are analyzed algebraically; mixed curvature/RR corrections are evaluated through an 11d lift and numerical extremization.

Approximate analytic evolution near the hilltop: linearize the field equations, use approximately constant H, extract an exponential growing mode, and conservatively estimate the acceleration duration before applying the TCC.

Numerically evolve the exact cosine force and Friedmann equation from rest at the hilltop, adding independent stochastic field jumps. The reported boundary uses fewer than half of simulations violating the TCC; the figure caption quotes ±0.01 Mpl precision in f_eff.

Quintessence simulations evolve classical axions from zero velocity at early redshift with dust-like matter. Present day is defined by Ω_m=0.3 and Ω_φ=0.7, and predicted w_φ(z) is compared with the paper's adopted observational upper bound.

For even h, differentiate the Hessian determinant polynomial to obtain a symmetric h-array, viewed as a bilinear map on Sym^(h/2)(H). Its determinant is called SymDet; rank and signature remain useful when the determinant vanishes.
